Electron Spin

What you need to know

  • A charge that circulates is a magnet. An electron with orbital angular momentum L⃗\vec{L}L has a magnetic moment μ⃗=−(e/2me) L⃗\vec{\mu} = -(e/2m_e)\,\vec{L}μ​=−(e/2me​)L, so μz=−μBml\mu_z = -\mu_Bm_lμz​=−μB​ml​ with the Bohr magneton μB=eℏ/2me=5.79×10−5\mu_B = e\hbar/2m_e = 5.79\times10^{-5}μB​=eℏ/2me​=5.79×10−5 eV/T. A magnetic field BBB along zzz shifts each state by μBB ml\mu_BB\,m_lμB​Bml​ and splits a level into 2l+12l + 12l+1: the Zeeman effect.

  • Stern and Gerlach sent silver atoms through a non-uniform magnetic field, which sorts atoms by μz\mu_zμz​. Silver’s outer electron has l=0l = 0l=0, so one undeflected spot was expected. The beam split in two.

  • The electron carries an angular momentum of its own, spin, with s=12s = \frac{1}{2}s=21​. It has two states, α\alphaα (ms=+12m_s = +\frac{1}{2}ms​=+21​) and β\betaβ (ms=−12m_s = -\frac{1}{2}ms​=−21​), with Sz=±12ℏS_z = \pm\frac{1}{2}\hbarSz​=±21​ℏ and length 32ℏ\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar23​​ℏ. Spin obeys the commutators of L⃗^\hat{\vec{L}}L^ but is not a motion in space: its states are two-component vectors and its operators 2×22\times22×2 matrices, the smallest quantum system there is.

  • The spin magnetic moment is μz=−geμBms\mu_z = -g_e\mu_Bm_sμz​=−ge​μB​ms​ with ge=2.0023g_e = 2.0023ge​=2.0023, twice as magnetic as orbital motion. In a field the two spin states lie geμBBg_e\mu_BBge​μB​B apart, the basis of EPR (electrons, GHz) and NMR (nuclei, MHz).

  • With spin, a hydrogen state has four quantum numbers, nnn, lll, mlm_lml​, msm_sms​, and level nnn holds 2n22n^22n2 states. Spin-orbit coupling, A L⃗^⋅S⃗^/ℏ2A\,\hat{\vec{L}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}}/\hbar^2AL^⋅S^/ℏ2, ties the two angular momenta together: only the total J⃗^=L⃗^+S⃗^\hat{\vec{J}} = \hat{\vec{L}} + \hat{\vec{S}}J^=L^+S^ stays sharp, with j=l±12j = l \pm \frac{1}{2}j=l±21​, and every level with l>0l > 0l>0 splits in two (fine structure), named by term symbols such as 2P3/2^2P_{3/2}2P3/2​. Sodium’s yellow line is a doublet for this reason. Light drives transitions with Δl=±1\Delta l = \pm1Δl=±1 and Δms=0\Delta m_s = 0Δms​=0.

A moving charge is a magnet¶

The Schrödinger equation of Lectures 5.1 and 5.2 treated the electron as a charged point mass. This lecture adds magnetism: first the magnetism of the electron’s orbital motion, which that equation already contains, and then a second kind, which it does not.

Three symbols change their meaning for this lecture. μ\muμ is a magnetic moment (the reduced mass does not appear; the electron mass mem_eme​ stands in for it, a 0.05% difference in hydrogen). BBB is the strength of a magnetic field in tesla. And the quantum number mmm of Lectures 4.4 to 5.2 is written mlm_lml​ from here on, because a second mmm is coming.

A loop of current¶

Take the model system of Lecture 4.4: a particle of mass mmm and charge qqq moving at speed vvv on a circle of radius rrr. It passes any point of the circle once per period T=2πr/vT = 2\pi r/vT=2πr/v, so it is an electric current. A loop of current III around an area is a magnet, and the strength of the magnet, its magnetic moment, is the current times the area:

I=qT=qv2πrcharge passing per unit timeμ=I⋅πr2=qvr2current times area=q2m (mvr)=q2m LL=mvr on a circle (Lecture 4.4)\begin{aligned} I &= \frac{q}{T} = \frac{qv}{2\pi r} && \text{charge passing per unit time}\\[4pt] \mu &= I\cdot\pi r^2 = \frac{qvr}{2} && \text{current times area}\\[4pt] &= \frac{q}{2m}\,(mvr) = \frac{q}{2m}\,L && L = mvr \text{ on a circle (Lecture 4.4)} \end{aligned}Iμ​=Tq​=2πrqv​=I⋅πr2=2qvr​=2mq​(mvr)=2mq​L​​charge passing per unit timecurrent times areaL=mvr on a circle (Lecture 4.4)​
(1)

The moment is a vector along the axis of the loop, like L⃗\vec{L}L. For a positive charge the two are parallel. The electron’s charge is q=−eq = -eq=−e, so its moment points against its angular momentum:

μ⃗=−e2me L⃗\vec{\mu} = -\frac{e}{2m_e}\,\vec{L}μ​=−2me​e​L
(2)

# synced: current_loop
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
from scipy.special import ellipk, ellipe
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.7))
a, b = 1.5, 0.46                                             # the orbit: a circle of radius a seen at a tilt
# field lines of a circular current loop in the plane of the page: contours of the flux rho * A_phi
g = np.linspace(-3.6, 3.6, 361)
X, Z = np.meshgrid(g, np.linspace(-3.0, 3.0, 301))
rho = np.abs(X) + 1e-6
k2 = 4 * a * rho / ((a + rho)**2 + Z**2)
flux = np.sqrt(a * rho) * ((2 - k2) * ellipk(k2) - 2 * ellipe(k2)) / np.sqrt(k2)
ax.contour(X, Z, flux, levels=[0.12, 0.3, 0.6, 1.05, 1.7], colors="#ced4da", linewidths=1.1, zorder=0)
t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400)
ax.fill(a * np.cos(t), b * np.sin(t), color=PURPLE, alpha=0.07, lw=0, zorder=1)
ax.plot(a * np.cos(t), b * np.sin(t), color="#343a40", lw=2.0, zorder=2)
arrow = lambda p0, p1, col, lw, ms: ax.annotate("", xy=p1, xytext=p0, zorder=6, arrowprops=dict(
    arrowstyle="-|>", color=col, lw=lw, mutation_scale=ms, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
arrow((0, 0), (0, 2.05), PURPLE, 3.0, 20)                    # angular momentum, up for counterclockwise motion
arrow((0, 0), (0, -2.05), CARDINAL, 3.0, 20)                 # magnetic moment, opposite: the charge is negative
ax.text(0.18, 1.95, r"$\vec{L}$", fontsize=19, color=PURPLE, va="center")
ax.text(0.18, -1.95, r"$\vec{\mu}$", fontsize=19, color=CARDINAL, va="center")
f = np.radians(-58)                                          # the electron, on the near side of the orbit
pe = np.array([a * np.cos(f), b * np.sin(f)])
ax.plot([0, pe[0]], [0, pe[1]], color=GRAY, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=3)
ax.text(0.5, -0.07, r"$r$", fontsize=16, color=GRAY, ha="center", va="center")
tv = np.array([-a * np.sin(f), b * np.cos(f)]); tv = tv / np.hypot(*tv)
arrow(pe, pe + 1.0 * tv, TEAL, 2.4, 17)
ax.text(*(pe + 1.0 * tv + np.array([0.2, 0.05])), r"$\vec{v}$", fontsize=17, color=TEAL, va="center")
ax.plot(*pe, "o", color=TEAL, ms=12, zorder=7)
ax.text(pe[0] - 0.05, pe[1] - 0.36, r"$-e$", fontsize=16, color=TEAL, ha="center", va="center")
f2 = np.radians(118)                                         # the current runs against the electron
pc = np.array([a * np.cos(f2), b * np.sin(f2)])
tc = np.array([a * np.sin(f2), -b * np.cos(f2)]); tc = tc / np.hypot(*tc)
arrow(pc - 0.01 * tc, pc + 0.3 * tc, "#343a40", 2.0, 20)
ax.text(pc[0] - 0.12, pc[1] + 0.3, r"$I$", fontsize=17, color="#343a40", ha="center", va="center")
ax.set_xlim(-3.3, 3.3); ax.set_ylim(-2.75, 2.75); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.0, right=1.0, top=1.0, bottom=0.0)
plt.show()

Fig. An electron on a circular orbit. Its angular momentum L⃗\vec{L}L points up. The current III runs against the motion because the charge is negative, so the magnetic moment μ⃗\vec{\mu}μ​ points down. Gray: the magnetic field lines of the loop.

  • The orbit has dropped out. Neither rrr nor vvv survives: μ/L=q/2m\mu/L = q/2mμ/L=q/2m for any orbit. The ratio is called the magnetogyric ratio γ\gammaγ, and for an orbiting electron γ=−e/2me\gamma = -e/2m_eγ=−e/2me​.

  • The loop is a bar magnet. Its field lines leave one face and return to the other, with the north pole on the side μ⃗\vec{\mu}μ​ points to.

  • Light particles are strong magnets, since γ∝1/m\gamma \propto 1/mγ∝1/m. A proton with the same angular momentum is 1836 times less magnetic.

A magnet in a field¶

A magnet in a magnetic field B⃗\vec{B}B has the energy

E=−μ⃗⋅B⃗=−μzB(B⃗ along z)E = -\vec{\mu}\cdot\vec{B} = -\mu_zB \qquad (\vec{B} \text{ along } z)E=−μ​⋅B=−μz​B(B along z)
(3)

lowest when the moment points along the field, as a compass needle does. What the field does to the magnet depends on whether the field is the same everywhere:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
from matplotlib.patches import Polygon, Rectangle
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"wspace": 0.04})
arrow = lambda a_, p0, p1, col, lw, ms: a_.annotate("", xy=p1, xytext=p0, zorder=6, arrowprops=dict(
    arrowstyle="-|>", color=col, lw=lw, mutation_scale=ms, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
# a small bar magnet centred at (x0, 0): its moment (red arrow, S to N), the forces on its two poles, the net force.
# The field pushes the N pole along B (up) and the S pole against it (down), harder where B is stronger.
magnets = [(ax, 0.0, 1, 0.85, 0.85), (bx, -1.05, 1, 0.55, 1.15), (bx, 1.05, -1, 0.55, 1.15)]
for a_, x0, up, f_top, f_bot in magnets:
    a_.add_patch(Rectangle((x0 - 0.2, -0.62), 0.4, 1.24, fc="white", ec="#343a40", lw=1.6, zorder=4))
    arrow(a_, (x0, -0.48 * up), (x0, 0.5 * up), CARDINAL, 3.0, 17)
    a_.text(x0 - 0.38, 0.42 * up, "N", fontsize=14, ha="center", va="center", weight="bold", color="#343a40")
    a_.text(x0 - 0.38, -0.42 * up, "S", fontsize=14, ha="center", va="center", weight="bold", color="#343a40")
    for end, f in ((1, f_top), (-1, f_bot)):                 # end = +1 the top pole, -1 the bottom pole
        ends = [(x0, end * 0.68), (x0, end * (0.68 + f))]    # from the pole outward
        if up < 0:                                           # N below, S above: both forces point into the magnet, draw them pushing
            ends = ends[::-1]
        arrow(a_, ends[0], ends[1], GRAY, 2.0, 14)
    net = up * (f_top - f_bot)
    if abs(net) > 0.01:
        arrow(a_, (x0 + 0.6, -0.5 * np.sign(net)), (x0 + 0.6, 0.7 * np.sign(net)), "#212529", 4.2, 24)
        a_.text(x0 + 0.82, 0.1 * np.sign(net), r"$\vec{F}$", fontsize=18, va="center", color="#212529")
# left: a uniform field
for x in np.linspace(-2.4, 2.4, 9):
    ax.plot([x, x], [-2.3, 2.3], color="#ced4da", lw=1.2, zorder=0)
    arrow(ax, (x, 1.9), (x, 2.3), "#ced4da", 1.2, 11)
ax.text(2.62, 2.05, r"$\vec{B}$", fontsize=17, color=GRAY, va="center")
ax.set_title("uniform field", fontsize=14)
# right: the Stern-Gerlach magnet in cross-section, a sharp edge below and a groove above; B is strongest at the edge
bx.add_patch(Polygon([[-2.6, -2.9], [2.6, -2.9], [2.6, -2.45], [0, -1.75], [-2.6, -2.45]], fc="#dee2e6", ec=GRAY, lw=1.3, zorder=2))
th = np.linspace(np.pi, 2 * np.pi, 80)
top = [[-2.6, 2.9], [-2.6, 2.0]] + [[1.5 * np.cos(q), 2.0 - 0.62 * np.sin(q)] for q in th] + [[2.6, 2.0], [2.6, 2.9]]
bx.add_patch(Polygon(top, fc="#dee2e6", ec=GRAY, lw=1.3, zorder=2))
for xt in np.linspace(-1.35, 1.35, 9):                       # field lines fan out from the edge to the groove
    zz = np.linspace(0, 1, 60)
    zt = 2.0 + 0.62 * np.sqrt(max(0.0, 1 - (xt / 1.5)**2))
    xs = xt * (0.06 + 0.94 * zz**1.25)
    zs = (-1.75 + 0.33 * abs(xt)) + (zt - (-1.75 + 0.33 * abs(xt))) * zz
    bx.plot(xs, zs, color="#ced4da", lw=1.2, zorder=0)
    arrow(bx, (xs[-9], zs[-9]), (xs[-1], zs[-1]), "#ced4da", 1.2, 11)
bx.text(2.05, 1.55, r"$\vec{B}$", fontsize=17, color=GRAY, va="center")
bx.set_title("non-uniform field", fontsize=14)
for a_ in (ax, bx):
    a_.set_xlim(-3.0, 3.0); a_.set_ylim(-3.0, 3.0); a_.set_aspect("equal"); a_.axis("off")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.92, bottom=0.01)
plt.show()

Fig. A small magnet (red arrow: its moment, from the S pole to the N pole) in a field that points up. The field pushes the N pole along B⃗\vec{B}B and the S pole against it (gray arrows). Left: in a uniform field the two forces cancel. Right: between a sharp edge and a groove the field is stronger at the bottom, the two forces differ, and a net force F⃗\vec{F}F remains.

  • Uniform field: a twist, no push. The forces on the two poles are equal and opposite. They turn a tilted magnet but do not move it.

  • Non-uniform field: a net force. The pole in the stronger field is pushed harder. Since E=−μzBE = -\mu_zBE=−μz​B and force is minus the slope of the energy,

Fz=−∂E∂z=μz ∂B∂zF_z = -\frac{\partial E}{\partial z} = \mu_z\,\frac{\partial B}{\partial z}Fz​=−∂z∂E​=μz​∂z∂B​
(4)

  • The force sorts magnets by μz\mu_zμz​. A moment along the field is pulled toward the stronger field, a moment against the field is pushed away from it, and a moment at right angles feels nothing. This is the idea of the Stern-Gerlach experiment below.

An atom in a magnetic field¶

The orbital magnetic moment is quantized¶

The classical relation becomes an operator relation, μ^z=−(e/2me) L^z\hat{\mu}_z = -(e/2m_e)\,\hat{L}_zμ^​z​=−(e/2me​)L^z​, and the hydrogen states are eigenfunctions of L^z\hat{L}_zL^z​ with eigenvalues mlℏm_l\hbarml​ℏ (Lecture 4.4):

The orbital magnetic moment
μ⃗^=−e2me L⃗^,μz=−eℏ2me ml=−μB ml,ml=−l,…,l\hat{\vec{\mu}} = -\frac{e}{2m_e}\,\hat{\vec{L}}, \qquad \mu_z = -\frac{e\hbar}{2m_e}\,m_l = -\mu_B\,m_l, \qquad m_l = -l, \dots, lμ​^​=−2me​e​L^,μz​=−2me​eℏ​ml​=−μB​ml​,ml​=−l,…,l
(5)
μB=eℏ2me=9.274×10−24 J/T\mu_B = \frac{e\hbar}{2m_e} = 9.274\times10^{-24}\ \text{J/T}μB​=2me​eℏ​=9.274×10−24 J/T
(6)

  • μB\mu_BμB​ is the Bohr magneton, the magnetic moment that goes with one ℏ\hbarℏ of orbital angular momentum: the natural unit for the magnetism of electrons

  • μz\mu_zμz​ takes 2l+12l + 12l+1 values. An s electron (l=0l = 0l=0) has no orbital moment at all

The Bohr magneton in the units a chemist meets, for a field of one tesla (the Earth’s field is 5×10−55\times10^{-5}5×10−5 T, a refrigerator magnet about 10-2 T, an NMR magnet 10 to 20 T):

μB\mu_BμB​ asvaluewhat it sets
an energy per tesla5.788×10−55.788\times10^{-5}5.788×10−5 eV/Tthe shift of a level: 58 μ\muμeV in 1 T, against gaps of several eV between levels
a wavenumber per tesla, μB/hc\mu_B/hcμB​/hc0.467 cm−1^{-1}−1/Tthe shift of a spectral line
a frequency per tesla, μB/h\mu_B/hμB​/h14.0 GHz/Tthe frequency of a photon that connects two neighbouring magnetic levels
a temperature per tesla, μB/kB\mu_B/k_BμB​/kB​0.67 K/Tthe temperature below which a 1 T field lines up the moments

The Hamiltonian and its levels¶

A field along zzz adds the energy −μ^zB-\hat{\mu}_zB−μ^​z​B to the hydrogen Hamiltonian H^0\hat{H}_0H^0​ of Lecture 5.1:

H^=H^0+μBBℏ L^z\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \frac{\mu_BB}{\hbar}\,\hat{L}_zH^=H^0​+ℏμB​B​L^z​
(7)

There is no new equation to solve. L^z\hat{L}_zL^z​ commutes with H^0\hat{H}_0H^0​, so the states ψnlml\psi_{nlm_l}ψnlml​​ are eigenfunctions of both (Lecture 3.5b), and therefore of their sum:

H^ ψnlml=(En+μBB ml)ψnlml\hat{H}\,\psi_{nlm_l} = \left(E_n + \mu_BB\,m_l\right)\psi_{nlm_l}H^ψnlml​​=(En​+μB​Bml​)ψnlml​​
(8)
A hydrogenlike atom in a magnetic field (orbital motion only)
H^=H^0+μBBℏ L^z,Enml=En+μBB ml\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \frac{\mu_BB}{\hbar}\,\hat{L}_z, \qquad E_{nm_l} = E_n + \mu_BB\,m_lH^=H^0​+ℏμB​B​L^z​,Enml​​=En​+μB​Bml​
(9)

  • The states do not change. The field shifts each one in proportion to its mlm_lml​, which is why mlm_lml​ is called the magnetic quantum number

  • A level of angular momentum lll splits into 2l+12l + 12l+1 equally spaced levels, μBB\mu_BBμB​B apart

  • In Lecture 5.2 the zzz axis was our choice, and the atom could not tell. A field along zzz makes the direction matter: it gives each mlm_lml​ its own energy, so the states of definite mlm_lml​ stay stationary, while pxp_xpx​ and pyp_ypy​, which mix ml=+1m_l = +1ml​=+1 and -1, no longer are

The Zeeman effect¶

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.9), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.2, 1], "wspace": 0.1})
B = np.linspace(0, 1, 50)
E2, E1, s = 3.2, 0.0, 0.85                                   # schematic: the real 2p - 1s gap is 10^5 splittings
for m in (1, 0, -1):
    ax.plot(B, E2 + s * m * B, color=PURPLE, lw=2.6)
    ax.text(1.04, E2 + s * m, rf"$m_l = {m:+d}$" if m else r"$m_l = 0$", va="center", fontsize=13, color=PURPLE)

ax.text(1.04, E1, r"$m_l = 0$", va="center", fontsize=13, color=TEAL)
ax.text(-0.05, E2, "2p", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=15, color=PURPLE, weight="bold")
ax.text(-0.05, E1, "1s", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=15, color=TEAL, weight="bold")
for k, m in enumerate((-1, 0, 1)):                           # the three lines: Delta m_l = -1, 0, +1
    x = 0.66 + 0.11 * k
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x, E2 + s * m * x), xytext=(x, E1), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#495057", lw=1.8,
                                                                          mutation_scale=14, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
ax.set_xlim(-0.25, 1.42); ax.set_ylim(-0.5, 4.5)
ax.set_xticks([0]); ax.set_xticklabels(["0"], fontsize=11); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel(r"magnetic field $B$", fontsize=12.5); ax.set_ylabel("energy", fontsize=12.5)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_bounds(0, 1)
# the spectrum: one line without the field, three with it
for y0, lines in ((1.25, (0,)), (0.0, (-1, 0, 1))):
    bx.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((-2.2, y0), 4.4, 0.8, fc="#f1f3f5", ec="#ced4da", lw=1))
    for d in lines:
        bx.plot([d, d], [y0, y0 + 0.8], color="#495057", lw=3.2, solid_capstyle="butt")
bx.text(-2.35, 1.65, r"$B = 0$", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=13.5)
bx.text(-2.35, 0.4, r"$B > 0$", ha="right", va="center", fontsize=13.5)
bx.set_xlim(-3.6, 2.3); bx.set_ylim(-0.25, 2.3)
bx.set_xticks([-1, 0, 1]); bx.set_xticklabels([r"$\nu_0 - \mu_BB/h$", r"$\nu_0$", r"$\nu_0 + \mu_BB/h$"], fontsize=11.5)
bx.set_yticks([]); bx.spines["left"].set_visible(False); bx.spines["bottom"].set_bounds(-2.2, 2.2)

Fig. Left: in a magnetic field the 2p level splits into three levels μBB\mu_BBμB​B apart, and 1s does not move. The arrows are the three allowed transitions. Right: one spectral line becomes three.

  • One line becomes three. The line at ν0\nu_0ν0​ gains two companions at ν0±μBB/h\nu_0 \pm \mu_BB/hν0​±μB​B/h. Pieter Zeeman saw spectral lines widen in a magnetic field in 1896, and Hendrik Lorentz explained the triplet.

  • Three, whatever lll. Light changes mlm_lml​ by 0 or ±1\pm1±1 (the selection rules at the end of this lecture), and every level has the same spacing μBB\mu_BBμB​B. So 3d→2p3\text{d} \to 2\text{p}3d→2p, with five levels above and three below, still gives the same three frequencies. This is the normal Zeeman effect.

  • The splitting is small. At 1 T it is 5.8×10−55.8\times10^{-5}5.8×10−5 eV, against 10.2 eV for the line itself: six parts in a million.

  • Most atoms do not obey. The triplet is seen only for certain lines. Sodium’s yellow line, and hydrogen’s own lines in a weak field, split into four, six or more components with unequal spacings. This anomalous Zeeman effect had no explanation for a quarter of a century. What was missing is the subject of the rest of this lecture.

Example: how far apart are the Zeeman lines?

The red line of cadmium at 643.85 nm shows the normal triplet. How far from the center are its outer components in a field of 1.0 T?

Each outer component is shifted by

Δν~=μBBhc=0.467 cm−1\Delta\tilde{\nu} = \frac{\mu_BB}{hc} = 0.467\ \text{cm}^{-1}Δν~=hcμB​B​=0.467 cm−1
(10)

The line itself is at ν~0=1/λ=15 532\tilde{\nu}_0 = 1/\lambda = 15\,532ν~0​=1/λ=15532 cm−1^{-1}−1, so the shift is 3 parts in 105. In wavelength, from λ=1/ν~\lambda = 1/\tilde{\nu}λ=1/ν~,

∣Δλ∣=λ2 Δν~=(643.85×10−7 cm)2×0.467 cm−1=0.019 nm\lvert\Delta\lambda\rvert = \lambda^2\,\Delta\tilde{\nu} = (643.85\times10^{-7}\ \text{cm})^2\times0.467\ \text{cm}^{-1} = 0.019\ \text{nm}∣Δλ∣=λ2Δν~=(643.85×10−7 cm)2×0.467 cm−1=0.019 nm
(11)

Separating lines 0.02 nm apart at 644 nm takes a resolving power λ/Δλ\lambda/\Delta\lambdaλ/Δλ of about 30 000, ten times finer than the hydrogen and deuterium pair of Lecture 5.1. Zeeman’s first observation was only a broadening of the line.

The Stern-Gerlach experiment¶

In 1922 Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach measured the magnetic moment of single atoms with the force of the last section. They evaporated silver in an oven, cut a narrow beam of atoms out of the vapor with slits, sent it between the poles of a magnet shaped to make the field strongly non-uniform (a sharp edge facing a groove), and let the atoms land on a glass plate.

Source
# synced: stern_gerlach
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 3.5), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [4.3, 1], "wspace": 0.03})
xm0, xm1, xp, kk = 2.5, 5.5, 8.7, 0.043                     # magnet from xm0 to xm1, plate at xp; z = +-kk (x - xm0)^2 inside
n_fr, per, dx = 36, 3, 0.36                                  # frames, atoms launched per frame, distance per frame
N = n_fr * per
sgn = rng.choice([1, -1], N)                                 # which way each atom goes: decided only at the magnet
z0 = rng.normal(0, 0.03, N)
zland = rng.normal(0, 0.09, N)
yland = rng.uniform(-0.8, 0.8, N)
frac = rng.uniform(0, 1, N)
bend = lambda x: np.where(x < xm0, 0.0, np.where(x < xm1, (x - xm0)**2, (xm1 - xm0)**2 + 2 * (xm1 - xm0) * (x - xm1)))
zend = kk * float(bend(np.array(xp)))
ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0.0, -0.6), 1.05, 1.2, fc="#dee2e6", ec=GRAY, lw=1.3))
ax.text(0.52, -0.85, "oven", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12.5, color=GRAY)
for s in (1, -1):
    ax.plot([1.75, 1.75], [s * 0.2, s * 0.8], color=GRAY, lw=3.5, solid_capstyle="butt")
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((xm0, 0.62 if s > 0 else -1.62), xm1 - xm0, 1.0, fc="#dee2e6", ec=GRAY, lw=1.3))
ax.text(0.5 * (xm0 + xm1), 1.12, "magnet", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12.5, color=GRAY)
ax.plot([xp, xp], [-2.0, 2.0], color="#343a40", lw=4, solid_capstyle="butt")
ax.text(xp, -2.2, "plate", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12.5, color=GRAY)
xs = np.linspace(1.05, xp, 200)
for s, col in ((1, TEAL), (-1, ORANGE)):
    ax.plot(xs, s * kk * bend(xs), color=col, lw=1.0, alpha=0.35, zorder=1)
fly = ax.scatter([], [], s=26, zorder=5)
ax.set_xlim(-0.2, 9.1); ax.set_ylim(-2.6, 2.3); ax.axis("off")
bx.add_patch(Rectangle((-1.05, -2.0), 2.1, 4.0, fc="#f1f3f5", ec="#343a40", lw=1.6))
hits = bx.scatter([], [], s=20, zorder=5)
bx.text(0, -2.2, "plate, face on", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=12.5, color=GRAY)
bx.set_xlim(-1.5, 1.5); bx.set_ylim(-2.6, 2.3); bx.axis("off")
dark, cols = np.array([0.29, 0.31, 0.34, 1.0]), {1: np.array([0.063, 0.471, 0.584, 1.0]), -1: np.array([0.878, 0.482, 0.0, 1.0])}

def update(f):
    x = 1.05 + (f - np.arange(N) // per + frac) * dx          # how far each atom has flown by frame f
    on = (x >= 1.05) & (x < xp)
    z = z0 * (x < 1.75) + sgn * kk * bend(x)
    c = np.array([dark if xi < xm0 else cols[si] for xi, si in zip(x[on], sgn[on])]).reshape(-1, 4)
    fly.set_offsets(np.c_[x[on], z[on]]); fly.set_facecolors(c)
    done = x >= xp
    hits.set_offsets(np.c_[yland[done], sgn[done] * zend + zland[done]])
    hits.set_facecolors(np.array([cols[si] for si in sgn[done]]).reshape(-1, 4))

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.01, right=0.99, top=0.99, bottom=0.02)
ani = FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=n_fr, interval=100, blit=False)
plt.close(fig)
HTML(ani.to_jshtml())
Loading...

Fig. Atoms from the oven fly through a non-uniform magnetic field and land on a plate. Each atom is pushed up or down by a force proportional to its μz\mu_zμz​. The beam splits in two.

  • The apparatus measures μz\mu_zμz​, one atom at a time. The force Fz=μz ∂B/∂zF_z = \mu_z\,\partial B/\partial zFz​=μz​∂B/∂z turns a value of μz\mu_zμz​ into a position on the plate.

  • The atom is neutral. A magnetic field bends the path of a moving charge, which would swamp the effect. A neutral atom feels only the push on its moment.

What should the plate show?

Fig. What the plate would show for classical magnets, for atoms with l=0l = 0l=0 and for atoms with l=1l = 1l=1, and what Stern and Gerlach found for silver.

  • Classical magnets leave the oven pointing in every direction. μz\mu_zμz​ takes every value from −μ-\mu−μ to +μ+\mu+μ, and the beam smears into a band.

  • Orbital angular momentum gives μz=−μBml\mu_z = -\mu_Bm_lμz​=−μB​ml​ with 2l+12l + 12l+1 values, an odd number of spots: one for l=0l = 0l=0, three for l=1l = 1l=1.

  • Silver has one electron outside closed shells, in the 5s orbital, and closed shells carry no angular momentum (Chapter 7). So l=0l = 0l=0, and the prediction is a single spot in the middle.

  • Observed: two spots, and nothing in the middle. Two means 2l+1=22l + 1 = 22l+1=2, that is l=12l = \frac{1}{2}l=21​, which no orbital motion can have: lll is a whole number because eimϕe^{im\phi}eimϕ must join up around the circle (Lecture 4.4). The moment that splits the beam is not orbital. Hydrogen atoms in their 1s ground state split in two as well (Phipps and Taylor, 1927).

Example: how far apart are the two spots?

Silver atoms (mass 107.9 u) leave a 1300 K oven at about 550 m/s and cross a magnet 3.5 cm long in which the field changes by 10 T per centimeter. Each atom carries μz=±μB\mu_z = \pm\mu_Bμz​=±μB​ (shown below). How far sideways has it moved at the end of the magnet?

The force is tiny, but so is the mass:

F=μB ∂B∂z=9.27×10−24 J/T×1000 T/m=9.3×10−21 NF = \mu_B\,\frac{\partial B}{\partial z} = 9.27\times10^{-24}\ \text{J/T}\times1000\ \text{T/m} = 9.3\times10^{-21}\ \text{N}F=μB​∂z∂B​=9.27×10−24 J/T×1000 T/m=9.3×10−21 N
(12)
a=Fm=9.3×10−21 N1.79×10−25 kg=5.2×104 m/s2a = \frac{F}{m} = \frac{9.3\times10^{-21}\ \text{N}}{1.79\times10^{-25}\ \text{kg}} = 5.2\times10^{4}\ \text{m/s}^2a=mF​=1.79×10−25 kg9.3×10−21 N​=5.2×104 m/s2
(13)

The atom spends t=0.035 m/550 m/s=6.4×10−5t = 0.035\ \text{m}/550\ \text{m/s} = 6.4\times10^{-5}t=0.035 m/550 m/s=6.4×10−5 s in the magnet, and moves

z=12at2=12×5.2×104×(6.4×10−5)2 m=0.10 mmz = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\times5.2\times10^{4}\times(6.4\times10^{-5})^2\ \text{m} = 0.10\ \text{mm}z=21​at2=21​×5.2×104×(6.4×10−5)2 m=0.10 mm
(14)

The two beams end up 0.2 mm apart, which is what Stern and Gerlach saw under a microscope.

Watch: the experiment and what it means

Spin¶

A new angular momentum¶

Two spots mean a magnetic moment with two values of μz\mu_zμz​. In 1925 George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit proposed, to explain doubled lines in atomic spectra, that the electron carries an angular momentum of its own in addition to the orbital one. It is called spin. Count its states as for any angular momentum, 2s+1=22s + 1 = 22s+1=2:

s=12,ms=+12  or  −12s = \tfrac{1}{2}, \qquad m_s = +\tfrac{1}{2} \ \text{ or } \ -\tfrac{1}{2}s=21​,ms​=+21​  or  −21​
(15)

The spin operators S^x\hat{S}_xS^x​, S^y\hat{S}_yS^y​, S^z\hat{S}_zS^z​ are defined by obeying the commutation rules of angular momentum,

[S^x,S^y]=iℏ S^z,[S^y,S^z]=iℏ S^x,[S^z,S^x]=iℏ S^y[\hat{S}_x, \hat{S}_y] = i\hbar\,\hat{S}_z, \qquad [\hat{S}_y, \hat{S}_z] = i\hbar\,\hat{S}_x, \qquad [\hat{S}_z, \hat{S}_x] = i\hbar\,\hat{S}_y[S^x​,S^y​]=iℏS^z​,[S^y​,S^z​]=iℏS^x​,[S^z​,S^x​]=iℏS^y​
(16)

and everything that Lecture 4.4 drew from the commutators alone carries over: S^2=S^x2+S^y2+S^z2\hat{S}^2 = \hat{S}_x^2 + \hat{S}_y^2 + \hat{S}_z^2S^2=S^x2​+S^y2​+S^z2​ and one component can be sharp together, with eigenvalues s(s+1)ℏ2s(s+1)\hbar^2s(s+1)ℏ2 and msℏm_s\hbarms​ℏ. The ladder argument of that lecture (its “Going further” box) allowed ladders with half-integer lll. Orbital motion cannot use them. Spin does.

Electron spin
S^2α=34ℏ2 α,S^zα=+12ℏ α\hat{S}^2\alpha = \tfrac{3}{4}\hbar^2\,\alpha, \qquad \hat{S}_z\alpha = +\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\,\alphaS^2α=43​ℏ2α,S^z​α=+21​ℏα
(17)
S^2β=34ℏ2 β,S^zβ=−12ℏ β\hat{S}^2\beta = \tfrac{3}{4}\hbar^2\,\beta, \qquad \hat{S}_z\beta = -\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\,\betaS^2β=43​ℏ2β,S^z​β=−21​ℏβ
(18)
⟨α∣α⟩=⟨β∣β⟩=1,⟨α∣β⟩=0\langle\alpha|\alpha\rangle = \langle\beta|\beta\rangle = 1, \qquad \langle\alpha|\beta\rangle = 0⟨α∣α⟩=⟨β∣β⟩=1,⟨α∣β⟩=0
(19)

  • s=12s = \frac{1}{2}s=21​ for every electron, so S^2\hat{S}^2S^2 always gives s(s+1)ℏ2=34ℏ2s(s+1)\hbar^2 = \frac{3}{4}\hbar^2s(s+1)ℏ2=43​ℏ2: a spin of length 32ℏ\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar23​​ℏ

  • Two states: α\alphaα, “spin up”, with ms=+12m_s = +\frac{1}{2}ms​=+21​, and β\betaβ, “spin down”, with ms=−12m_s = -\frac{1}{2}ms​=−21​

  • They are orthonormal, as eigenstates of a Hermitian operator with different eigenvalues must be

  • Spin is intrinsic. Every electron has s=12s = \frac{1}{2}s=21​, as every electron has the charge −e-e−e and the mass mem_eme​. The orbital quantum number lll depends on the state the electron is in; sss cannot be changed. Only the orientation msm_sms​ can.

  • Spin is not a motion in space. α\alphaα and β\betaβ are not functions of xxx, yyy, zzz or of the angles. There is no Y1/2m(θ,ϕ)Y_{1/2}^{m}(\theta, \phi)Y1/2m​(θ,ϕ): a function of ϕ\phiϕ with m=12m = \frac{1}{2}m=21​ would change sign after one full turn. The name is historical.

  • The Schrödinger equation does not contain it. Our Hamiltonians were built by taking a classical energy and replacing xxx and ppp by operators, and spin has no classical energy to start from. It comes out on its own from Dirac’s relativistic equation for the electron (1928). Here it is added by hand, as a new degree of freedom with the properties in the box.

  • Other particles have spin too. Protons and neutrons have s=12s = \frac{1}{2}s=21​, the photon has s=1s = 1s=1, and nuclei have spins 0,12,1,32,…0, \frac{1}{2}, 1, \frac{3}{2}, \dots0,21​,1,23​,… Particles with half-integer spin are fermions and those with whole spin are bosons. That distinction is behind the Pauli principle and the periodic table (Chapter 7).

The vector model¶

Spin follows the rules that Lecture 4.4 found for L⃗\vec{L}L, with sss in place of lll and msm_sms​ in place of mlm_lml​. Draw the two side by side:

Example: is the electron a spinning ball?

Suppose the electron were a solid ball of radius r=2.8×10−15r = 2.8\times10^{-15}r=2.8×10−15 m (the “classical electron radius”) turning about its axis with angular momentum 12ℏ\frac{1}{2}\hbar21​ℏ. How fast would its equator move?

A solid sphere has I=25mer2I = \frac{2}{5}m_er^2I=52​me​r2, so L=Iω=25mer vL = I\omega = \frac{2}{5}m_er\,vL=Iω=52​me​rv with v=ωrv = \omega rv=ωr the speed at the equator:

v=5L2mer=5ℏ4mer=5×1.055×10−344×9.11×10−31×2.8×10−15 msv = \frac{5L}{2m_er} = \frac{5\hbar}{4m_er} = \frac{5\times1.055\times10^{-34}}{4\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times2.8\times10^{-15}}\ \frac{\text{m}}{\text{s}}v=2me​r5L​=4me​r5ℏ​=4×9.11×10−31×2.8×10−155×1.055×10−34​ sm​
(20)
v=5.2×1010 m/s≈170 cv = 5.2\times10^{10}\ \text{m/s} \approx 170\,cv=5.2×1010 m/s≈170c
(21)

Faster than light, 170 times over. Scattering experiments show that the electron is smaller than 10-18 m, which makes it thousands of times worse. Nothing is rotating. Spin is angular momentum, and it adds to L⃗\vec{L}L in the conservation law (below), but it is not the rotation of anything.

Spin states are two-component vectors¶

How should a spin state be written down? An orbital is a function of rrr, θ\thetaθ, ϕ\phiϕ, but spin has no coordinate to plot against. Three steps lead to the answer:

  1. Two readings, two eigenstates. A measurement of SzS_zSz​ has two outcomes, so S^z\hat{S}_zS^z​ has two eigenstates, α\alphaα and β\betaβ, and they are orthonormal (the box above).

  2. Every spin state is a superposition of the two. The eigenstates of an observable are a complete set of axes (Lecture 3.6), so any spin state is χ=cα α+cβ β\chi = c_\alpha\,\alpha + c_\beta\,\betaχ=cα​α+cβ​β, with cα=⟨α∣χ⟩c_\alpha = \langle\alpha|\chi\ranglecα​=⟨α∣χ⟩ and cβ=⟨β∣χ⟩c_\beta = \langle\beta|\chi\ranglecβ​=⟨β∣χ⟩.

  3. Two numbers make a column. In Lecture 3.5 a wavefunction became a long column of its values on a grid. A spin state needs two entries, cαc_\alphacα​ on top and cβc_\betacβ​ below. The state α\alphaα itself has cα=1c_\alpha = 1cα​=1 and cβ=0c_\beta = 0cβ​=0:

χ=cα α+cβ β=(cαcβ)⟹α=(10),β=(01)\chi = c_\alpha\,\alpha + c_\beta\,\beta = \begin{pmatrix}c_\alpha\\ c_\beta\end{pmatrix} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \alpha = \begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \beta = \begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\end{pmatrix}χ=cα​α+cβ​β=(cα​cβ​​)⟹α=(10​),β=(01​)
(22)
∣cα∣2+∣cβ∣2=1\lvert c_\alpha\rvert^2 + \lvert c_\beta\rvert^2 = 1∣cα​∣2+∣cβ​∣2=1
(23)

With only two components, spin is the simplest quantum system there is, and Lectures 3.5 and 3.6 apply to it in full with nothing larger than a 2×22\times22×2 matrix.

  • The bracket is a dot product, row times column with the bra’s components conjugated: ⟨α∣β⟩=1⋅0+0⋅1=0\langle\alpha|\beta\rangle = 1\cdot0 + 0\cdot1 = 0⟨α∣β⟩=1⋅0+0⋅1=0. There is no integral, because there is no coordinate. (Some books write a formal integral over a “spin variable”, and the states as ψ+1/2\psi_{+1/2}ψ+1/2​ and ψ−1/2\psi_{-1/2}ψ−1/2​. They mean this two-term sum.)

  • The Born rule of Lecture 3.6: a measurement of SzS_zSz​ gives +12ℏ+\frac{1}{2}\hbar+21​ℏ with probability ∣cα∣2\lvert c_\alpha\rvert^2∣cα​∣2 and −12ℏ-\frac{1}{2}\hbar−21​ℏ with probability ∣cβ∣2\lvert c_\beta\rvert^2∣cβ​∣2.

Spin operators are 2×22\times22×2 matrices¶

If a state is a column of two numbers, an operator that turns one state into another is a 2×22\times22×2 matrix (Lecture 3.5). The matrix of S^z\hat{S}_zS^z​ needs no calculation: α\alphaα and β\betaβ are its eigenvectors, and a matrix written in the basis of its own eigenvectors is diagonal, with the eigenvalues on the diagonal:

S^z=ℏ2(100−1)\hat{S}_z = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}S^z​=2ℏ​(10​0−1​)
(24)

The other two components are not diagonal in this basis. Together the three are 12ℏ\frac{1}{2}\hbar21​ℏ times the Pauli matrices:

S^x=ℏ2(0110),S^y=ℏ2(0−ii0),S^z=ℏ2(100−1)\hat{S}_x = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \hat{S}_y = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0 & -i\\ i & 0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \hat{S}_z = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}S^x​=2ℏ​(01​10​),S^y​=2ℏ​(0i​−i0​),S^z​=2ℏ​(10​0−1​)
(25)
Example: S^z\hat{S}_zS^z​ and S^x\hat{S}_xS^x​ acting on α\alphaα and β\betaβ

Multiply each matrix into the columns, row times column.

S^z α=ℏ2(100−1)(10)=ℏ2(1⋅1+0⋅00⋅1−1⋅0)=ℏ2(10)=+12ℏ α\hat{S}_z\,\alpha = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1\cdot1 + 0\cdot0\\ 0\cdot1 - 1\cdot0\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix} = +\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\,\alphaS^z​α=2ℏ​(10​0−1​)(10​)=2ℏ​(1⋅1+0⋅00⋅1−1⋅0​)=2ℏ​(10​)=+21​ℏα
(26)
S^z β=ℏ2(100−1)(01)=ℏ2(0−1)=−12ℏ β\hat{S}_z\,\beta = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -1\end{pmatrix} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\,\betaS^z​β=2ℏ​(10​0−1​)(01​)=2ℏ​(0−1​)=−21​ℏβ
(27)

The matrix gives back the two eigenvalue equations the lecture started from. Now the same with S^x\hat{S}_xS^x​:

S^x α=ℏ2(0110)(10)=ℏ2(01)=12ℏ β\hat{S}_x\,\alpha = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 0\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 1\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\,\betaS^x​α=2ℏ​(01​10​)(10​)=2ℏ​(01​)=21​ℏβ
(28)

Not a multiple of α\alphaα: S^x\hat{S}_xS^x​ turns spin up into spin down, so α\alphaα is not an eigenvector of S^x\hat{S}_xS^x​.

  • S^z\hat{S}_zS^z​ is diagonal because α\alphaα and β\betaβ, its own eigenvectors, are the basis. Its eigenvalues ±12ℏ\pm\frac{1}{2}\hbar±21​ℏ sit on the diagonal (Lecture 3.5).

  • S^x\hat{S}_xS^x​ flips the spin. Row times column gives S^xα=12ℏ β\hat{S}_x\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\hbar\,\betaS^x​α=21​ℏβ and S^xβ=12ℏ α\hat{S}_x\beta = \frac{1}{2}\hbar\,\alphaS^x​β=21​ℏα. So α\alphaα is not an eigenvector of S^x\hat{S}_xS^x​: when SzS_zSz​ is sharp, SxS_xSx​ is not.

  • Each matrix is Hermitian, equal to its own conjugate transpose, which is why S^y\hat{S}_yS^y​ needs its two iii’s, as momentum did in Lecture 3.5b. Each has the eigenvalues ±12ℏ\pm\frac{1}{2}\hbar±21​ℏ: whatever axis the spin is measured along, the reading is +12ℏ+\frac{1}{2}\hbar+21​ℏ or −12ℏ-\frac{1}{2}\hbar−21​ℏ.

  • The square of each matrix is 14ℏ2\frac{1}{4}\hbar^241​ℏ2 times the unit matrix, so S^2=34ℏ2\hat{S}^2 = \frac{3}{4}\hbar^2S^2=43​ℏ2 times the unit matrix: every spin state is an eigenstate of S^2\hat{S}^2S^2, as the box says.

operatoracting on α\alphaαacting on β\betaβ
S^z\hat{S}_zS^z​+12ℏ α+\frac{1}{2}\hbar\,\alpha+21​ℏα−12ℏ β-\frac{1}{2}\hbar\,\beta−21​ℏβ
S^x\hat{S}_xS^x​12ℏ β\frac{1}{2}\hbar\,\beta21​ℏβ12ℏ α\frac{1}{2}\hbar\,\alpha21​ℏα
S^y\hat{S}_yS^y​i2ℏ β\frac{i}{2}\hbar\,\beta2i​ℏβ−i2ℏ α-\frac{i}{2}\hbar\,\alpha−2i​ℏα

The same checks in numpy, in units of ℏ\hbarℏ:

import numpy as np

# spin matrices in the basis (alpha, beta)
Sx = 0.5 * np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
Sy = 0.5 * np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]])
Sz = 0.5 * np.array([[1, 0], [0, -1]])

print("Sx Sy - Sy Sx = i Sz ?", np.allclose(Sx @ Sy - Sy @ Sx, 1j * Sz))
print("S^2 =\n", (Sx @ Sx + Sy @ Sy + Sz @ Sz).real)

# measure Sx: its possible readings and the states they leave
values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(Sx)
print("readings of Sx:", values)
print("their states (columns):\n", vectors.round(3))
Sx Sy - Sy Sx = i Sz ? True
S^2 =
 [[0.75 0.  ]
 [0.   0.75]]
readings of Sx: [-0.5  0.5]
their states (columns):
 [[-0.707  0.707]
 [ 0.707  0.707]]
Example: measure SxS_xSx​ on a spin-up electron

An electron is in the state α\alphaα. What can a measurement of SxS_xSx​ give, and how often?

The readings are the eigenvalues of S^x\hat{S}_xS^x​. From det⁡(S^x−λ)=λ2−14ℏ2=0\det(\hat{S}_x - \lambda) = \lambda^2 - \frac{1}{4}\hbar^2 = 0det(S^x​−λ)=λ2−41​ℏ2=0 they are λ=±12ℏ\lambda = \pm\frac{1}{2}\hbarλ=±21​ℏ, with eigenvectors (check them by row times column)

χ+x=12(11)=α+β2,χ−x=12(1−1)=α−β2\chi_{+x} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ 1\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\alpha + \beta}{\sqrt{2}}, \qquad \chi_{-x} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ -1\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\alpha - \beta}{\sqrt{2}}χ+x​=2​1​(11​)=2​α+β​,χ−x​=2​1​(1−1​)=2​α−β​
(29)

The probabilities are the squared components of α\alphaα along them (Lecture 3.6):

P(±12ℏ)=∣⟨χ±x∣α⟩∣2=(12)2=12P\left(\pm\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\right) = \lvert\langle\chi_{\pm x}|\alpha\rangle\rvert^2 = \left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}P(±21​ℏ)=∣⟨χ±x​∣α⟩∣2=(2​1​)2=21​
(30)

A spin that is certainly up along zzz is a coin toss along xxx, and ⟨Sx⟩=0\langle S_x\rangle = 0⟨Sx​⟩=0 as the vector model said. After the reading +12ℏ+\frac{1}{2}\hbar+21​ℏ the electron is in χ+x\chi_{+x}χ+x​, which is half α\alphaα and half β\betaβ: the certainty about SzS_zSz​ is gone. (The matrix is the σx\sigma_xσx​ of Appendix A.3.)

One magnet after another¶

A Stern-Gerlach magnet measures one component of the spin, and blocking one of its two beams prepares a state. Put several in a row and the measurement postulates of Lecture 3.6 become things one can see on a plate:

Source
# synced: sg_sequence
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
from matplotlib.patches import Rectangle, FancyBboxPatch
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.6, 4.4))
w, hgt, gap = 1.25, 0.9, 2.55                                 # analyser width and height, spacing
rows = [("(a)", 2.5, ["z", "z"], [("+z", "100%"), ("-z", "0")]),
        ("(b)", 0.0, ["z", "x"], [("+x", "50%"), ("-x", "50%")]),
        ("(c)", -2.5, ["z", "x", "z"], [("+z", "50%"), ("-z", "50%")])]
for tag, y, axes_, outs in rows:
    ax.text(-0.75, y, tag, fontsize=14.5, ha="center", va="center", color="#343a40")
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((-0.3, y - 0.3), 0.75, 0.6, fc="#dee2e6", ec=GRAY, lw=1.2))
    if tag == "(a)":
        ax.text(0.08, y - 0.42, "oven", fontsize=12, ha="center", va="top", color=GRAY)
    ax.plot([0.45, 1.6], [y, y], color="#495057", lw=2.2)
    for i, name in enumerate(axes_):
        x0 = 1.6 + gap * i
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x0, y - hgt / 2), w, hgt, boxstyle="round,pad=0,rounding_size=0.12", fc="white", ec="#343a40", lw=1.8, zorder=3))
        ax.text(x0 + w / 2, y, f"${name}$", fontsize=20, ha="center", va="center", zorder=4)
        last = i == len(axes_) - 1
        if not last:                                         # keep the + beam, block the - beam
            ax.plot([x0 + w, x0 + w + 0.45, x0 + gap], [y + 0.25, y + 0.25, y], color=TEAL, lw=2.4, zorder=2)
            ax.plot([x0 + w, x0 + w + 0.5], [y - 0.25, y - 0.25], color=ORANGE, lw=2.4, zorder=2)
            ax.plot([x0 + w + 0.5, x0 + w + 0.5], [y - 0.5, y - 0.02], color="#343a40", lw=4.5, solid_capstyle="butt", zorder=3)
        else:
            for (lab, pct), sgn, col in zip(outs, (1, -1), (TEAL, ORANGE)):
                none = pct == "0"
                ax.annotate("", xy=(x0 + w + 1.0, y + sgn * 0.25), xytext=(x0 + w, y + sgn * 0.25), zorder=2,
                            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="#ced4da" if none else col, lw=2.4, mutation_scale=16,
                                            shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0, ls=(0, (3, 2)) if none else "-"))
                ax.text(x0 + w + 1.15, y + sgn * 0.3, f"${lab}$", fontsize=15, va="center", color=GRAY if none else col)
                ax.text(x0 + w + 1.85, y + sgn * 0.3, pct, fontsize=15, va="center", weight="bold", color=GRAY if none else col)
ax.set_xlim(-1.1, 10.6); ax.set_ylim(-3.3, 3.3); ax.axis("off")
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.0, right=1.0, top=1.0, bottom=0.0)
plt.show()

Fig. Stern-Gerlach magnets in a row. Each box measures the spin along the axis written in it, and its lower beam is blocked. (a) zzz, then zzz. (b) zzz, then xxx. (c) zzz, then xxx, then zzz again.

  • (a) Measure twice, same answer. The first magnet leaves the atoms it passes in α\alphaα. A second measurement of SzS_zSz​ gives +12ℏ+\frac{1}{2}\hbar+21​ℏ every time: the collapse of Lecture 3.6, and the reason a measurement can be trusted.

  • (b) A sharp SzS_zSz​ is an undecided SxS_xSx​. Half of the atoms come out +x+x+x and half −x-x−x, as in the example above. No way of preparing the beam makes both sharp, because [S^z,S^x]≠0[\hat{S}_z, \hat{S}_x] \neq 0[S^z​,S^x​]=0 (Lecture 3.5b).

  • (c) Measuring SxS_xSx​ erases the zzz result. The atoms leaving the second magnet are in χ+x=(α+β)/2\chi_{+x} = (\alpha + \beta)/\sqrt{2}χ+x​=(α+β)/2​, and the third magnet finds +z+z+z and −z-z−z half the time each, although every one of these atoms had passed a “+z+z+z only” filter. A measurement does not read off a value the atom already had. It leaves the atom in an eigenstate of what was measured.

Send atoms through. Set the second magnet along zzz, xxx or −z-z−z, or tilt it by any angle: the fraction found +++ along a magnet tilted by θ\thetaθ is cos⁡2(θ/2)\cos^2(\theta/2)cos2(θ/2) (Problem 3). Then add the third magnet.

The magnetic moment of spin¶

If spin is an angular momentum, it should come with a magnetic moment, as orbital motion does. It does, with twice the ratio:

The spin magnetic moment
μ⃗^s=−ge e2me S⃗^,μz=−ge μB ms≈∓μB,ge=2.0023\hat{\vec{\mu}}_s = -g_e\,\frac{e}{2m_e}\,\hat{\vec{S}}, \qquad \mu_z = -g_e\,\mu_B\,m_s \approx \mp\mu_B, \qquad g_e = 2.0023μ​^​s​=−ge​2me​e​S^,μz​=−ge​μB​ms​≈∓μB​,ge​=2.0023
(31)
E=−μzB=ge μBB ms=±12 ge μBBE = -\mu_zB = g_e\,\mu_BB\,m_s = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}\,g_e\,\mu_BBE=−μz​B=ge​μB​Bms​=±21​ge​μB​B
(32)

  • geg_ege​ is the electron’s g factor. Orbital motion has g=1g = 1g=1: for the same angular momentum, spin is twice as magnetic

  • μz≈∓μB\mu_z \approx \mp\mu_Bμz​≈∓μB​: half a unit of angular momentum, a whole Bohr magneton

  • In a field along zzz the state β\betaβ, whose moment points along the field, lies below α\alphaα, and the two are geμBBg_e\mu_BBge​μB​B apart

  • This is what Stern and Gerlach measured. Silver’s 5s electron has no orbital moment, so the moment of the atom is the spin moment of that one electron: μz=±μB\mu_z = \pm\mu_Bμz​=±μB​, two spots.

  • Where the 2 comes from. Dirac’s equation gives g=2g = 2g=2 exactly. The extra 0.0023 comes from quantum electrodynamics, and the measured and calculated values of geg_ege​ agree to 12 digits, the most precise agreement between theory and experiment in science.

Two levels in a field: magnetic resonance¶

Source
# synced: spin_resonance
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.9), gridspec_kw={"wspace": 0.72})
# (panel, slope of the splitting in frequency per tesla, largest field, field of the arrow, its label, m label, which state is lower)
panels = [(ax, 2.0023 * 13.996, 0.5, 0.34, "9.5 GHz", "m_s", -1), (bx, 42.577, 12.0, 9.4, "400 MHz", "m_I", 1)]
for a_, slope, Bmax, B0, lab, mname, low in panels:
    B = np.linspace(0, Bmax, 50)
    for m, col, name in ((0.5, TEAL, r"\alpha"), (-0.5, ORANGE, r"\beta")):

                fontsize=13, va="center")
    a_.annotate("", xy=(B0, 0.5 * slope * B0), xytext=(B0, -0.5 * slope * B0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<|-|>", color="#343a40",
                                                                                     lw=1.8, mutation_scale=14, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
    a_.text(B0 - 0.03 * Bmax, 0, lab, fontsize=13.5, ha="right", va="center", color="#343a40",
            bbox=dict(fc="white", ec="none", pad=1.5))
    a_.set_xlim(0, Bmax); a_.set_ylim(-0.6 * slope * Bmax, 0.6 * slope * Bmax)
    a_.set_xlabel(r"magnetic field $B$ (T)", fontsize=12); a_.tick_params(labelsize=10.5)

Fig. The two spin states of an electron (left) and of a proton (right) in a magnetic field. The arrows mark the photon that flips the spin, at 0.34 T for the electron and at 9.4 T for the proton.

  • EPR. An unpaired electron in a field BBB absorbs a photon with hν=geμBBh\nu = g_e\mu_BBhν=ge​μB​B, 28 GHz per tesla: microwaves. Electron paramagnetic resonance detects whatever has an unpaired electron: radicals, many transition-metal ions, defects in solids.

  • NMR. The proton also has spin 12\frac{1}{2}21​ (written III for a nucleus). Its moment is set by the nuclear magneton μN=eℏ/2mp=μB/1836\mu_N = e\hbar/2m_p = \mu_B/1836μN​=eℏ/2mp​=μB​/1836 and its own g factor, gp=5.586g_p = 5.586gp​=5.586: hν=gpμNBh\nu = g_p\mu_NBhν=gp​μN​B, 42.6 MHz per tesla, radio waves. A “400 MHz” spectrometer is a 9.4 T magnet. The proton’s charge is positive, so its moment lies along its spin and α\alphaα is the lower state.

  • Same physics, 660 times apart in frequency, because of the mass in μ=(q/2m)L\mu = (q/2m)Lμ=(q/2m)L.

  • Why chemists care. In both, the exact frequency depends slightly on the surroundings of the spin: the electrons around a nucleus shield it from the field by a few parts per million (the chemical shift). That small dependence turns a spin into a reporter of structure.

Example: the microwaves that flip an electron spin

A free radical sits in a field of 0.34 T. What frequency and wavelength of radiation flips its unpaired spin?

ν=ge μBBh=2.0023×14.0 GHzT×0.34 T=9.5 GHz\nu = \frac{g_e\,\mu_BB}{h} = 2.0023\times14.0\ \frac{\text{GHz}}{\text{T}}\times0.34\ \text{T} = 9.5\ \text{GHz}ν=hge​μB​B​=2.0023×14.0 TGHz​×0.34 T=9.5 GHz
(33)
λ=cν=3.1 cm\lambda = \frac{c}{\nu} = 3.1\ \text{cm}λ=νc​=3.1 cm
(34)

Centimeter waves, the “X band” of radar, which is why most EPR spectrometers work at this field. The photon energy is hν=3.9×10−5h\nu = 3.9\times10^{-5}hν=3.9×10−5 eV, 650 times smaller than kBTk_BTkB​T at room temperature, so the two spin states are almost equally populated (Problem 1).

The complete states of hydrogen¶

The spatial wavefunction says where the electron is, and the spin state says how its spin points. As long as the two do not influence each other, a complete state is their product, a spin orbital:

ψnlmlms=Rnl(r) Ylml(θ,ϕ)×{αms=+12βms=−12or∣n,l,ml,ms⟩\psi_{nlm_lm_s} = R_{nl}(r)\,Y_l^{m_l}(\theta, \phi)\times\begin{cases}\alpha & m_s = +\frac{1}{2}\\[2pt] \beta & m_s = -\frac{1}{2}\end{cases} \qquad \text{or} \qquad |n, l, m_l, m_s\rangleψnlml​ms​​=Rnl​(r)Ylml​​(θ,ϕ)×{αβ​ms​=+21​ms​=−21​​or∣n,l,ml​,ms​⟩
(35)
operatoreigenvaluequantum number
H^0\hat{H}_0H^0​−Z2Eh/2n2-Z^2E_h/2n^2−Z2Eh​/2n2n=1,2,3,…n = 1, 2, 3, \dotsn=1,2,3,…
L^2\hat{L}^2L^2l(l+1) ℏ2l(l+1)\,\hbar^2l(l+1)ℏ2l=0,1,…,n−1l = 0, 1, \dots, n - 1l=0,1,…,n−1
L^z\hat{L}_zL^z​ml ℏm_l\,\hbarml​ℏml=−l,…,lm_l = -l, \dots, lml​=−l,…,l
S^2\hat{S}^2S^234ℏ2\frac{3}{4}\hbar^243​ℏ2s=12s = \frac{1}{2}s=21​, always
S^z\hat{S}_zS^z​ms ℏm_s\,\hbarms​ℏms=+12,−12m_s = +\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}ms​=+21​,−21​

  • Four quantum numbers. The five operators commute with one another (the spin operators act on α\alphaα and β\betaβ only, the others on rrr, θ\thetaθ, ϕ\phiϕ only), so one state carries all five values. Four numbers label it, since sss never changes.

  • Orthonormal. The bracket of two spin orbitals is the integral over space times the dot product of the spin parts. Two states with the same orbital and opposite spins are orthogonal because ⟨α∣β⟩=0\langle\alpha|\beta\rangle = 0⟨α∣β⟩=0.

  • 2n22n^22n2 states in level nnn: 2, 8, 18, 32. With the Pauli principle these become the lengths of the rows of the periodic table (Chapter 7).

  • In a magnetic field both moments contribute: H^=H^0+μBBℏ(L^z+geS^z)\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \dfrac{\mu_BB}{\hbar}\left(\hat{L}_z + g_e\hat{S}_z\right)H^=H^0​+ℏμB​B​(L^z​+ge​S^z​), with energies En+μBB (ml+gems)E_n + \mu_BB\,(m_l + g_e m_s)En​+μB​B(ml​+ge​ms​). This is right as long as the two magnets inside the atom ignore each other. They do not quite.

Spin-orbit coupling¶

The electron sees a moving nucleus¶

Source
# synced: spin_orbit_frames
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.9), gridspec_kw={"wspace": 0.02})
a, b = 1.6, 0.5
t = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 400)
arrow = lambda a_, p0, p1, col, lw, ms: a_.annotate("", xy=p1, xytext=p0, zorder=6, arrowprops=dict(
    arrowstyle="-|>", color=col, lw=lw, mutation_scale=ms, shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
f = np.radians(-52)
pe = np.array([a * np.cos(f), b * np.sin(f)])
tv = np.array([-a * np.sin(f), b * np.cos(f)]); tv = tv / np.hypot(*tv)
for a_ in (ax, bx):
    a_.fill(a * np.cos(t), b * np.sin(t), color=PURPLE, alpha=0.06, lw=0, zorder=1)
    a_.plot(a * np.cos(t), b * np.sin(t), color="#868e96", lw=1.6, zorder=2)
    a_.set_xlim(-2.6, 2.6); a_.set_ylim(-1.75, 2.2); a_.set_aspect("equal"); a_.axis("off")
# left: the nucleus at rest, the electron circles it
ax.plot(0, 0, "o", color="#343a40", ms=13, zorder=7)
ax.text(-0.12, -0.36, r"$+Ze$", fontsize=14.5, color="#343a40", ha="center", va="center")
ax.plot(*pe, "o", color=TEAL, ms=9, zorder=7)
ax.text(pe[0] + 0.02, pe[1] - 0.33, r"$-e$", fontsize=14.5, color=TEAL, ha="center", va="center")
arrow(ax, pe, pe + 0.85 * tv, TEAL, 2.2, 15)
arrow(ax, (0, 0), (0, 1.75), PURPLE, 3.0, 19)
ax.text(0.16, 1.62, r"$\vec{L}$", fontsize=18, color=PURPLE, va="center")
ax.set_title("nucleus at rest", fontsize=14)
# right: the electron at rest; the nucleus circles it the same way, a loop of positive current whose field is along L
f2 = np.radians(-128)
pn = np.array([a * np.cos(f2), b * np.sin(f2)])
tn = np.array([-a * np.sin(f2), b * np.cos(f2)]); tn = tn / np.hypot(*tn)
bx.plot(*pn, "o", color="#343a40", ms=13, zorder=7)
bx.text(pn[0] - 0.1, pn[1] - 0.38, r"$+Ze$", fontsize=14.5, color="#343a40", ha="center", va="center")
arrow(bx, pn, pn + 0.85 * tn, "#343a40", 2.2, 15)
arrow(bx, (-0.62, -0.1), (-0.62, 1.75), GRAY, 3.0, 19)
bx.text(-0.78, 1.62, r"$\vec{B}$", fontsize=18, color=GRAY, va="center", ha="right")
bx.plot(0, 0, "o", color=TEAL, ms=9, zorder=7)
arrow(bx, (0, 0), (0, 1.2), TEAL, 2.8, 17)
bx.text(0.16, 1.1, r"$\vec{S}$", fontsize=18, color=TEAL, va="center")
arrow(bx, (0, 0), (0, -1.2), CARDINAL, 2.8, 17)
bx.text(0.16, -1.12, r"$\vec{\mu}_s$", fontsize=18, color=CARDINAL, va="center")
bx.text(0.2, -0.02, r"$-e$", fontsize=14.5, color=TEAL, ha="left", va="center")

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.0, right=1.0, top=0.92, bottom=0.0)

Fig. Left: the electron orbits the nucleus, with orbital angular momentum L⃗\vec{L}L. Right: the same motion seen from the electron. The nucleus circles the electron, and this loop of positive current makes a magnetic field B⃗\vec{B}B at the electron, parallel to L⃗\vec{L}L. The spin moment μ⃗s\vec{\mu}_sμ​s​ has an energy in that field.

Seen from the electron, the nucleus is a loop of current, and a loop of current makes a magnetic field at its center. That field points along L⃗\vec{L}L and falls off as Z/r3Z/r^3Z/r3. The spin moment has the energy −μ⃗s⋅B⃗-\vec{\mu}_s\cdot\vec{B}−μ​s​⋅B in it, and with μ⃗s∝−S⃗\vec{\mu}_s \propto -\vec{S}μ​s​∝−S and B⃗∝L⃗\vec{B} \propto \vec{L}B∝L this is

H^so=ξ(r)  L⃗^⋅S⃗^,ξ(r)=Ze28πε0 me2c2 1r3\hat{H}_{\text{so}} = \xi(r)\;\hat{\vec{L}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}}, \qquad \xi(r) = \frac{Ze^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0\,m_e^2c^2}\,\frac{1}{r^3}H^so​=ξ(r)L^⋅S^,ξ(r)=8πε0​me2​c2Ze2​r31​
(36)

  • No outside field is involved. The atom makes the field itself. In hydrogen’s 2p state it is about 0.4 T (Problem 5).

  • ξ>0\xi > 0ξ>0: the energy is higher when S⃗\vec{S}S is parallel to L⃗\vec{L}L, because then the moment points against the internal field.

  • An s electron has no orbital motion (l=0l = 0l=0): no internal field, no coupling.

  • The c2c^2c2 marks a relativistic effect. It is small in light atoms and grows quickly with the nuclear charge.

In a state with radial function RnlR_{nl}Rnl​, the factor ξ(r)\xi(r)ξ(r) is replaced by its average, and it is convenient to absorb the ℏ2\hbar^2ℏ2 of L⃗^⋅S⃗^\hat{\vec{L}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}}L^⋅S^ into one constant with the units of energy, the spin-orbit coupling constant A=ℏ2⟨ξ⟩nlA = \hbar^2\langle\xi\rangle_{nl}A=ℏ2⟨ξ⟩nl​ of the level:

H^so=Aℏ2  L⃗^⋅S⃗^\hat{H}_{\text{so}} = \frac{A}{\hbar^2}\;\hat{\vec{L}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}}H^so​=ℏ2A​L^⋅S^
(37)

Only the total angular momentum is conserved¶

Written out, L⃗^⋅S⃗^=L^xS^x+L^yS^y+L^zS^z\hat{\vec{L}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}} = \hat{L}_x\hat{S}_x + \hat{L}_y\hat{S}_y + \hat{L}_z\hat{S}_zL^⋅S^=L^x​S^x​+L^y​S^y​+L^z​S^z​. The first two terms do not commute with L^z\hat{L}_zL^z​ or with S^z\hat{S}_zS^z​: the internal field twists the spin, the spin twists the orbit back, and neither mlm_lml​ nor msm_sms​ stays sharp. But nothing twists the atom as a whole, and by the rule of Lecture 4.4 (no torque, no change) its total angular momentum is conserved:

J⃗^=L⃗^+S⃗^,[H^,J^2]=[H^,J^z]=0\hat{\vec{J}} = \hat{\vec{L}} + \hat{\vec{S}}, \qquad [\hat{H}, \hat{J}^2] = [\hat{H}, \hat{J}_z] = 0J^=L^+S^,[H^,J^2]=[H^,J^z​]=0
(38)

J⃗^\hat{\vec{J}}J^ obeys the commutation rules of an angular momentum, so it has quantum numbers of its own: J^2\hat{J}^2J^2 gives j(j+1)ℏ2j(j+1)\hbar^2j(j+1)ℏ2 and J^z\hat{J}_zJ^z​ gives mjℏm_j\hbarmj​ℏ with mj=−j,…,jm_j = -j, \dots, jmj​=−j,…,j. Since J^z=L^z+S^z\hat{J}_z = \hat{L}_z + \hat{S}_zJ^z​=L^z​+S^z​, the projections add: mj=ml+msm_j = m_l + m_smj​=ml​+ms​.

The energy follows without solving anything. Square the sum (the cross terms combine because every component of L⃗^\hat{\vec{L}}L^ commutes with every component of S⃗^\hat{\vec{S}}S^):

J^2=L^2+S^2+2 L⃗^⋅S⃗^⟹L⃗^⋅S⃗^=12(J^2−L^2−S^2)\hat{J}^2 = \hat{L}^2 + \hat{S}^2 + 2\,\hat{\vec{L}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \hat{\vec{L}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\hat{J}^2 - \hat{L}^2 - \hat{S}^2\right)J^2=L^2+S^2+2L^⋅S^⟹L^⋅S^=21​(J^2−L^2−S^2)
(39)

In a state with sharp jjj, lll and sss each operator on the right gives its eigenvalue:

Spin-orbit coupling and the total angular momentum
J⃗^=L⃗^+S⃗^,j=l+12  or  l−12,mj=−j,…,j\hat{\vec{J}} = \hat{\vec{L}} + \hat{\vec{S}}, \qquad j = l + \tfrac{1}{2} \ \text{ or } \ l - \tfrac{1}{2}, \qquad m_j = -j, \dots, jJ^=L^+S^,j=l+21​  or  l−21​,mj​=−j,…,j
(40)
Eso=A2[j(j+1)−l(l+1)−s(s+1)]E_{\text{so}} = \frac{A}{2}\Big[j(j+1) - l(l+1) - s(s+1)\Big]Eso​=2A​[j(j+1)−l(l+1)−s(s+1)]
(41)
Eso=+12A l  (j=l+12),Eso=−12A (l+1)  (j=l−12)E_{\text{so}} = +\tfrac{1}{2}A\,l \ \ \left(j = l + \tfrac{1}{2}\right), \qquad E_{\text{so}} = -\tfrac{1}{2}A\,(l+1) \ \ \left(j = l - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)Eso​=+21​Al  (j=l+21​),Eso​=−21​A(l+1)  (j=l−21​)
(42)

  • For l=0l = 0l=0 there is only j=12j = \frac{1}{2}j=21​, and no splitting

  • AAA is the spin-orbit coupling constant of the level, an energy

  • The states of sharp energy are labelled by nnn, lll, jjj, mjm_jmj​. Neither mlm_lml​ nor msm_sms​ is sharp in them

  • Every level with l>0l > 0l>0 splits in two, 12A (2l+1)\frac{1}{2}A\,(2l+1)21​A(2l+1) apart: the fine structure

Adding l=1l = 1l=1 and s=12s = \frac{1}{2}s=21​: count the states¶

Why j=l±12j = l \pm \frac{1}{2}j=l±21​ and nothing else? Count, for the six states of a p electron:

Source

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.6, 3.9), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.25, 1], "wspace": 0.05})
frac = lambda k: (r"+" if k > 0 else r"-") + rf"\frac{{{abs(k)}}}{{2}}"          # k halves, as a signed fraction

for i, ml in enumerate((1, 0, -1)):
    ax.text(i * cw + cw / 2, 2 * ch + 0.28, rf"$m_l = {ml:+d}$" if ml else r"$m_l = 0$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=14, color=PURPLE)
    for j, ms2 in enumerate((1, -1)):                        # ms2 = 2 m_s

            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, y0), cw, ch, fc=PURPLE, alpha=0.75, lw=0))
        else:                                                # m_j = +-1/2 occurs twice: shared between j = 3/2 and j = 1/2
            ax.add_patch(Polygon([[x0, y0], [x0 + cw, y0 + ch], [x0, y0 + ch]], fc=PURPLE, alpha=0.75, lw=0))
            ax.add_patch(Polygon([[x0, y0], [x0 + cw, y0], [x0 + cw, y0 + ch]], fc=LIGHT, alpha=0.9, lw=0))

for j, (ms2, col) in enumerate(((1, TEAL), (-1, ORANGE))):

    bx.text(xc, 2.05, rf"$j = \frac{{{j2}}}{{2}}$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=16, color=PURPLE if j2 == 3 else "#8566c2")
for mj2 in (3, 1, -1, -3):

Fig. Left: the six states of a p electron sorted by mlm_lml​ and msm_sms​; each box shows mj=ml+msm_j = m_l + m_smj​=ml​+ms​. Right: the same six values of mjm_jmj​ form a ladder of four (j=32j = \frac{3}{2}j=23​) and a ladder of two (j=12j = \frac{1}{2}j=21​).

  • The largest mjm_jmj​ is 32\frac{3}{2}23​, and it occurs once. A ladder that reaches 32\frac{3}{2}23​ has j=32j = \frac{3}{2}j=23​, and it uses one state at each of 32,12,−12,−32\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{3}{2}23​,21​,−21​,−23​.

  • What is left is one state at +12+\frac{1}{2}+21​ and one at −12-\frac{1}{2}−21​: a ladder with j=12j = \frac{1}{2}j=21​.

  • 3×2=6=4+23\times2 = 6 = 4 + 23×2=6=4+2. The same six states, regrouped: a change of axes within the level, like the step from Y1±1Y_1^{\pm1}Y1±1​ to pxp_xpx​, pyp_ypy​ in Lecture 5.2. In general 2(2l+1)=(2l+2)+2l2(2l+1) = (2l+2) + 2l2(2l+1)=(2l+2)+2l, the two ladders j=l+12j = l + \frac{1}{2}j=l+21​ and j=l−12j = l - \frac{1}{2}j=l−21​.

  • The corner boxes are single products, for example Y1+1αY_1^{+1}\alphaY1+1​α for mj=+32m_j = +\frac{3}{2}mj​=+23​. The split boxes are shared: the state with j=32j = \frac{3}{2}j=23​, mj=12m_j = \frac{1}{2}mj​=21​ is 23  Y10 α+13  Y1+1 β\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\;Y_1^{0}\,\alpha + \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\;Y_1^{+1}\,\beta32​​Y10​α+31​​Y1+1​β, a superposition in which neither mlm_lml​ nor msm_sms​ is sharp but their sum is.

Example: an f electron

What values of jjj can an electron with l=3l = 3l=3 have, how many states are in each level, and where do the levels lie?

j=3+12=72j = 3 + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{7}{2}j=3+21​=27​ or 3−12=523 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{2}3−21​=25​, with 2j+1=82j + 1 = 82j+1=8 and 6 states: 8+6=14=2×78 + 6 = 14 = 2\times78+6=14=2×7, every state accounted for. From the box, Eso=+32AE_{\text{so}} = +\frac{3}{2}AEso​=+23​A for j=72j = \frac{7}{2}j=27​ and −2A-2A−2A for j=52j = \frac{5}{2}j=25​, a gap of 72A\frac{7}{2}A27​A. The weighted average is 8×32A+6×(−2A)=08\times\frac{3}{2}A + 6\times(-2A) = 08×23​A+6×(−2A)=0: the coupling splits the level without moving its center.

Fine structure and term symbols¶

The levels are named by a term symbol,

2s+1Lj^{2s+1}L_j2s+1Lj​
(43)

where LLL is the capital letter of lll (S, P, D, F for l=0,1,2,3l = 0, 1, 2, 3l=0,1,2,3), the superscript 2s+1=22s + 1 = 22s+1=2 counts the orientations of the spin (read “doublet”), and the subscript is jjj. Mind the letter S: in 2S1/2^2S_{1/2}2S1/2​ it means l=0l = 0l=0, not spin.

Fig. Left: spin-orbit coupling splits the six states of a p level into 2P3/2^2P_{3/2}2P3/2​ (four states) and 2P1/2^2P_{1/2}2P1/2​ (two). Right: the yellow line of sodium is two lines 0.60 nm apart.

  • Sodium’s yellow light is 3p→3s3\text{p} \to 3\text{s}3p→3s. The upper level is split and the lower one is not, so there are two lines: D2_22​ from 2P3/2^2P_{3/2}2P3/2​ at 588.995 nm and D1_11​ from 2P1/2^2P_{1/2}2P1/2​ at 589.592 nm.

  • In hydrogen the splitting is fine indeed. The 2p level splits by 0.365 cm−1^{-1}−1, or 4.5×10−54.5\times10^{-5}4.5×10−5 eV, the “10-4 eV” promised in Lecture 5.1. It turns Hα\alphaα into a doublet 0.014 nm wide, ten times closer than the hydrogen and deuterium pair.

  • It grows steeply with the nuclear charge: as Z4Z^4Z4 for hydrogenlike ions, and down a group of the periodic table.

atomlevellines (nm)doublet splitting (cm−1^{-1}−1)
Li2p670.78, 670.790.34
Na3p589.00, 589.5917.2
K4p766.49, 769.9057.7
Rb5p780.03, 794.76237.6
Cs6p852.11, 894.35554.0

  • In heavy atoms spin-orbit coupling is chemistry. It reaches tenths of an eV, lets states of different total spin mix, and with that opens the “spin-forbidden” paths of photochemistry: phosphorescence and intersystem crossing are faster when a heavy atom is near.

Example: the sodium D lines

From the two wavelengths, find the splitting of sodium’s 3p level and its coupling constant.

ν~2−ν~1=107588.995−107589.592=16 978.1−16 960.9=17.2 cm−1\tilde{\nu}_2 - \tilde{\nu}_1 = \frac{10^7}{588.995} - \frac{10^7}{589.592} = 16\,978.1 - 16\,960.9 = 17.2\ \text{cm}^{-1}ν~2​−ν~1​=588.995107​−589.592107​=16978.1−16960.9=17.2 cm−1
(44)

or 2.1 meV. Both lines end on the same 3s level, so the difference is the gap between 2P3/2^2P_{3/2}2P3/2​ and 2P1/2^2P_{1/2}2P1/2​, which is 32A\frac{3}{2}A23​A:

A=23×17.2 cm−1=11.5 cm−1A = \tfrac{2}{3}\times17.2\ \text{cm}^{-1} = 11.5\ \text{cm}^{-1}A=32​×17.2 cm−1=11.5 cm−1
(45)

47 times hydrogen’s 2p value, although sodium’s outer electron sees a nucleus screened by ten inner electrons. The 3p electron dips inside the core, and close to the nucleus, where 1/r31/r^31/r3 is large, it feels almost the full charge Z=11Z = 11Z=11.

Going further: hydrogen’s fine structure, exactly

For a hydrogenlike atom the average of 1/r31/r^31/r3 (the radial averages of Lecture 5.1) gives the coupling constant in closed form,

A=Z4Eh2 (137.04)2  n3 l (l+12)(l+1)A = \frac{Z^4E_h}{2\,(137.04)^2\;n^3\,l\,(l + \frac{1}{2})(l + 1)}A=2(137.04)2n3l(l+21​)(l+1)Z4Eh​​
(46)

where 1/137.041/137.041/137.04 is the fine-structure constant e2/4πε0ℏce^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar ce2/4πε0​ℏc, the speed of the electron in hydrogen’s ground state as a fraction of the speed of light. For 2p, A=Eh/(48×137.042)=3.0×10−5A = E_h/(48\times137.04^2) = 3.0\times10^{-5}A=Eh​/(48×137.042)=3.0×10−5 eV, and the splitting is 32A=4.5×10−5\frac{3}{2}A = 4.5\times10^{-5}23​A=4.5×10−5 eV =0.365= 0.365=0.365 cm−1^{-1}−1 =10.9= 10.9=10.9 GHz.

Two more relativistic corrections have the same size (the mass of a fast electron grows, and a term that acts only on s states). Added together, the three give a simple result, the one Dirac’s equation also gives:

Enj=En[1+Z2(137.04)2 n2(nj+12−34)]E_{nj} = E_n\left[1 + \frac{Z^2}{(137.04)^2\,n^2}\left(\frac{n}{j + \frac{1}{2}} - \frac{3}{4}\right)\right]Enj​=En​[1+(137.04)2n2Z2​(j+21​n​−43​)]
(47)

The energy depends on nnn and jjj, not on lll: 2 2S1/22\,{}^2S_{1/2}22S1/2​ and 2 2P1/22\,{}^2P_{1/2}22P1/2​ coincide, and 2 2P3/22\,{}^2P_{3/2}22P3/2​ lies 0.365 cm−1^{-1}−1 above them. In 1947 Willis Lamb and Robert Retherford found that 2 2S1/22\,{}^2S_{1/2}22S1/2​ in fact lies 1058 MHz (0.035 cm−1^{-1}−1) above 2 2P1/22\,{}^2P_{1/2}22P1/2​. This Lamb shift was the starting point of quantum electrodynamics. Smaller again is the hyperfine structure, the coupling of the electron’s moment to the proton’s (Problem 7).

Weak field or strong field¶

Now put the atom, spin-orbit coupling included, into a magnetic field. Two magnetic energies compete, the internal one of size AAA and the external one of size μBB\mu_BBμB​B (with geg_ege​ rounded to 2):

H^=H^0+Aℏ2 L⃗^⋅S⃗^+μBBℏ(L^z+2S^z)\hat{H} = \hat{H}_0 + \frac{A}{\hbar^2}\,\hat{\vec{L}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}} + \frac{\mu_BB}{\hbar}\left(\hat{L}_z + 2\hat{S}_z\right)H^=H^0​+ℏ2A​L^⋅S^+ℏμB​B​(L^z​+2S^z​)
(48)

The two added terms do not commute with each other, so no single set of labels fits every field. For a p level, though, the whole problem is a 6×66\times66×6 matrix, and its eigenvalues can be followed from one limit to the other:

Source
# synced: zeeman_crossover
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
LIGHT = "#b9a3dc"
Lz = np.diag([1.0, 0.0, -1.0])                               # l = 1 in the basis m_l = +1, 0, -1
Lp = np.sqrt(2) * np.diag([1.0, 1.0], 1)                     # L+ raises m_l
Sz = np.diag([0.5, -0.5])                                    # s = 1/2 in the basis alpha, beta
Sp = np.diag([1.0], 1)                                       # S+ turns beta into alpha
LS = np.kron(Lz, Sz) + 0.5 * (np.kron(Lp, Sp.T) + np.kron(Lp.T, Sp))   # L.S = Lz Sz + (L+ S- + L- S+)/2, units of hbar^2
Zm = np.kron(Lz, np.eye(2)) + 2 * np.kron(np.eye(3), Sz)     # Lz + 2 Sz
mj2 = np.rint(2 * np.diag(np.kron(Lz, np.eye(2)) + np.kron(np.eye(3), Sz))).astype(int)
b = np.linspace(0, 3, 301)                                   # mu_B B / A
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.6, 4.6))
ax.axvspan(0, 0.35, color="#f1f3f5", lw=0, zorder=0)
for k in (3, 1, -1, -3):                                     # m_j stays sharp at every field: diagonalize block by block
    idx = np.where(mj2 == k)[0]
    E = np.array([np.linalg.eigvalsh((LS + x * Zm)[np.ix_(idx, idx)]) for x in b])
    for c in range(len(idx)):
        upper = len(idx) == 1 or c == 1                      # the branch that starts in j = 3/2
        ax.plot(b, E[:, c], color=PURPLE if upper else LIGHT, lw=2.6)
for y, lab, col in ((0.5, r"$^2$P$_{3/2}$", PURPLE), (-1.0, r"$^2$P$_{1/2}$", "#8566c2")):
    ax.text(-0.07, y, lab, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=17, color=col)
ends = [(6.5, "+2"), (3.14, "+1"), (-0.47, r"0, 0"), (-3.19, "-1"), (-5.5, "-2")]
for y, lab in ends:
    ax.text(3.07, y, rf"${lab}$", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=17, color="#343a40")
ax.text(3.07, 7.6, r"$m_l + 2m_s$", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=16.5, color="#343a40")
ax.text(0.175, 7.6, "weak", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=15, color=GRAY)
ax.text(2.4, 7.6, "strong field", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=15, color=GRAY)
ax.set_xlim(0, 3); ax.set_ylim(-6.3, 8.2)
ax.set_xlabel(r"magnetic field, $\mu_BB/A$", fontsize=14.5); ax.set_ylabel(r"energy / $A$", fontsize=14.5)
ax.set_yticks([-4, -2, 0, 2, 4, 6]); ax.tick_params(labelsize=12.5)
ax.spines["left"].set_position(("outward", 74)); ax.spines["left"].set_bounds(-6, 6.5)

Fig. The six states of a p level in a magnetic field. Energies are in units of the spin-orbit constant AAA, and the field is given as μBB/A\mu_BB/AμB​B/A. Dark: the states that start in 2P3/2^2P_{3/2}2P3/2​. Light: those that start in 2P1/2^2P_{1/2}2P1/2​.

  • Weak field, μBB≪A\mu_BB \ll AμB​B≪A. The internal coupling wins. L⃗\vec{L}L and S⃗\vec{S}S stay locked into J⃗\vec{J}J, and the field splits each level into its 2j+12j + 12j+1 states of different mjm_jmj​: four from 2P3/2^2P_{3/2}2P3/2​, two from 2P1/2^2P_{1/2}2P1/2​. The states of one level are evenly spaced, but the spacing differs from level to level, so a spectral line breaks into many components with unequal gaps. This is the anomalous Zeeman effect. It was anomalous only as long as spin was unknown.

  • Strong field, μBB≫A\mu_BB \gg AμB​B≫A. The external field wins. L⃗\vec{L}L and S⃗\vec{S}S each line up with it on their own, mlm_lml​ and msm_sms​ are sharp again, and E=μBB (ml+2ms)E = \mu_BB\,(m_l + 2m_s)E=μB​B(ml​+2ms​): five levels for a p electron. Because light does not flip the spin, the spin part of the shift is the same before and after a transition, and the lines form the normal triplet again.

  • In between only mjm_jmj​ is sharp. The curves bend, and two states with the same mjm_jmj​ repel each other instead of crossing.

  • Which is which? μBB=A\mu_BB = AμB​B=A at 0.5 T for hydrogen’s 2p level and at 25 T for sodium’s 3p. A 1 T laboratory magnet is a strong field for hydrogen and a weak one for sodium.

Going further: the Landé factor, and the matrix behind the figure

Weak field. The energies are E=gj μBB mjE = g_j\,\mu_BB\,m_jE=gj​μB​Bmj​ with the Landé factor

gj=1+j(j+1)+s(s+1)−l(l+1)2 j(j+1)g_j = 1 + \frac{j(j+1) + s(s+1) - l(l+1)}{2\,j(j+1)}gj​=1+2j(j+1)j(j+1)+s(s+1)−l(l+1)​
(49)
level2S1/2^2S_{1/2}2S1/2​2P1/2^2P_{1/2}2P1/2​2P3/2^2P_{3/2}2P3/2​2D3/2^2D_{3/2}2D3/2​2D5/2^2D_{5/2}2D5/2​
gjg_jgj​223\frac{2}{3}32​43\frac{4}{3}34​45\frac{4}{5}54​65\frac{6}{5}56​

It lies between the orbital value 1 and the spin value 2. The field couples to L^z+2S^z=J^z+S^z\hat{L}_z + 2\hat{S}_z = \hat{J}_z + \hat{S}_zL^z​+2S^z​=J^z​+S^z​; in a state of sharp jjj the first part gives mjℏm_j\hbarmj​ℏ, and the second gives the part of S⃗\vec{S}S that lies along J⃗\vec{J}J, which the squaring trick supplies: S⃗^⋅J⃗^=12(J^2+S^2−L^2)\hat{\vec{S}}\cdot\hat{\vec{J}} = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{J}^2 + \hat{S}^2 - \hat{L}^2)S^⋅J^=21​(J^2+S^2−L^2).

The matrix. The six product states (ml,ms)(m_l, m_s)(ml​,ms​) are the basis. np.kron(A, B) builds the matrix of “operator AAA on the orbit, operator BBB on the spin”, and L^xS^x+L^yS^y=12(L^+S^−+L^−S^+)\hat{L}_x\hat{S}_x + \hat{L}_y\hat{S}_y = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{L}_+\hat{S}_- + \hat{L}_-\hat{S}_+)L^x​S^x​+L^y​S^y​=21​(L^+​S^−​+L^−​S^+​) with the raising and lowering operators of Lecture 4.4:

import numpy as np

# l = 1 in the basis m_l = +1, 0, -1; s = 1/2 in the basis alpha, beta (units of hbar)
Lz = np.diag([1.0, 0, -1])
Lp = np.sqrt(2) * np.diag([1.0, 1.0], 1)        # L+ raises m_l
Sz = np.diag([0.5, -0.5])
Sp = np.diag([1.0], 1)                          # S+ turns beta into alpha

LS = np.kron(Lz, Sz) + 0.5 * (np.kron(Lp, Sp.T) + np.kron(Lp.T, Sp))
field = np.kron(Lz, np.eye(2)) + 2 * np.kron(np.eye(3), Sz)     # Lz + 2 Sz

for b in (0, 0.1, 10):                          # b = mu_B B / A
    print(b, np.linalg.eigvalsh(LS + b * field).round(2))
# 0    [-1.   -1.    0.5   0.5   0.5   0.5 ]
# 0.1  [-1.03 -0.97  0.3   0.43  0.57  0.7 ]
# 10   [-19.5 -10.05 -0.55 -0.45 10.05 20.5]

At zero field the eigenvalues are -1 twice and +12+\frac{1}{2}+21​ four times, the box above for l=1l = 1l=1. In the weak field (b=0.1b = 0.1b=0.1) the levels are evenly spaced within each group, by gjbg_jbgj​b: 23×0.1\frac{2}{3}\times0.132​×0.1 and 43×0.1\frac{4}{3}\times0.134​×0.1. In the strong field (b=10b = 10b=10) they approach b (ml+2ms)=−20,−10,0,0,10,20b\,(m_l + 2m_s) = -20, -10, 0, 0, 10, 20b(ml​+2ms​)=−20,−10,0,0,10,20.

Which transitions light can drive¶

The electric field of light acts on the electron’s position, as it acted on a bond’s dipole in Lectures 4.3 and 4.5. A transition between two states is allowed only if the transition dipole ⟨ψf∣ r⃗ ∣ψi⟩\langle\psi_f|\,\vec{r}\,|\psi_i\rangle⟨ψf​∣r∣ψi​⟩ is not zero (Lecture 6.3), and for the states of a one-electron atom the integral over the angles decides:

Selection rules for a one-electron atom
Δl=±1,Δml=0,±1,Δms=0,Δn anything\Delta l = \pm1, \qquad \Delta m_l = 0, \pm1, \qquad \Delta m_s = 0, \qquad \Delta n \ \text{anything}Δl=±1,Δml​=0,±1,Δms​=0,Δn anything
(50)
with spin-orbit coupling:Δj=0,±1,Δmj=0,±1\text{with spin-orbit coupling:} \qquad \Delta j = 0, \pm1, \qquad \Delta m_j = 0, \pm1with spin-orbit coupling:Δj=0,±1,Δmj​=0,±1
(51)

  • Δl=±1\Delta l = \pm1Δl=±1: a photon carries one unit of angular momentum

  • Δms=0\Delta m_s = 0Δms​=0: the electric field of light acts on where the electron is, not on its spin

  • No rule for nnn: every nnnp state can fall to 1s, which is the whole Lyman series

The Balmer line Hα\alphaα (n=3→2n = 3 \to 2n=3→2) is three transitions at once, 3s→2p3\text{s} \to 2\text{p}3s→2p, 3p→2s3\text{p} \to 2\text{s}3p→2s and 3d→2p3\text{d} \to 2\text{p}3d→2p, which coincide in hydrogen because the energy does not depend on lll.

Parity says the same in the manner of Lecture 4.2: zzz is odd, YlmY_l^mYlm​ has parity (−1)l(-1)^l(−1)l, so lll must change by an odd number.

  • The Δml\Delta m_lΔml​ rule made the Zeeman triplet: Δml=0\Delta m_l = 0Δml​=0 for light polarized along the field, ±1\pm1±1 for the two circular polarizations.

  • An excited atom can only fall along the arrows.

Example: why 2s outlives 2p

The 2s and 2p states of hydrogen have the same energy, 10.2 eV above the ground state. An atom in 2p emits a Lyman α\alphaα photon within 1.6 ns: 2p→1s2\text{p} \to 1\text{s}2p→1s has Δl=−1\Delta l = -1Δl=−1. For an atom in 2s the only lower state is 1s, and 2s→1s2\text{s} \to 1\text{s}2s→1s has Δl=0\Delta l = 0Δl=0. Both states are even, zzz is odd, the integrand ψ1s z ψ2s\psi_{1s}\,z\,\psi_{2s}ψ1s​zψ2s​ is odd, and the transition dipole vanishes.

The atom is stuck. The 2s state is metastable: left alone it lasts 0.12 s, about 108 times longer than 2p, and then decays by a much slower process, the emission of two photons at once. In a real gas a collision usually comes first.
