Problems¶

Problem 1: Why NMR needs a big magnet¶

A proton has gp=5.586g_p = 5.586gp​=5.586, and the nuclear magneton is μN=5.051×10−27\mu_N = 5.051\times10^{-27}μN​=5.051×10−27 J/T. (a) Find the frequency that flips a proton spin in a 9.4 T magnet. (b) At 298 K, how many more protons per million are in the lower spin state than in the upper one? (c) Repeat (b) for an electron spin at 0.34 T. (d) Why do NMR spectroscopists pay for ever stronger magnets?

Solution

(a) The two states are gpμNBg_p\mu_NBgp​μN​B apart:

ν=gp μNBh=5.586×5.051×10−27 J/T×9.4 T6.626×10−34 J s=400 MHz\nu = \frac{g_p\,\mu_NB}{h} = \frac{5.586\times5.051\times10^{-27}\ \text{J/T}\times9.4\ \text{T}}{6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s}} = 400\ \text{MHz}ν=hgp​μN​B​=6.626×10−34 J s5.586×5.051×10−27 J/T×9.4 T​=400 MHz
(52)

(b) ΔE=hν=2.65×10−25\Delta E = h\nu = 2.65\times10^{-25}ΔE=hν=2.65×10−25 J and kBT=4.11×10−21k_BT = 4.11\times10^{-21}kB​T=4.11×10−21 J, so ΔE/kBT=6.4×10−5\Delta E/k_BT = 6.4\times10^{-5}ΔE/kB​T=6.4×10−5. The Boltzmann ratio is Nupper/Nlower=e−ΔE/kBT≈1−ΔE/kBTN_{\text{upper}}/N_{\text{lower}} = e^{-\Delta E/k_BT} \approx 1 - \Delta E/k_BTNupper​/Nlower​=e−ΔE/kB​T≈1−ΔE/kB​T, and the excess as a fraction of all spins is

Nlower−NupperNlower+Nupper≈ΔE2kBT=3.2×10−5\frac{N_{\text{lower}} - N_{\text{upper}}}{N_{\text{lower}} + N_{\text{upper}}} \approx \frac{\Delta E}{2k_BT} = 3.2\times10^{-5}Nlower​+Nupper​Nlower​−Nupper​​≈2kB​TΔE​=3.2×10−5
(53)

32 protons in a million. The rest cancel in pairs: for every spin that absorbs a photon, another emits one.

(c) For the electron ΔE=geμBB=6.3×10−24\Delta E = g_e\mu_BB = 6.3\times10^{-24}ΔE=ge​μB​B=6.3×10−24 J, ΔE/kBT=1.5×10−3\Delta E/k_BT = 1.5\times10^{-3}ΔE/kB​T=1.5×10−3, and the excess is 7.7×10−47.7\times10^{-4}7.7×10−4: 770 per million, 24 times better than NMR although the magnet is 28 times weaker.

(d) The net signal comes from the excess, which grows in proportion to BBB, and each photon carries an energy that also grows with BBB. A stronger magnet also spreads the chemical shifts over more hertz, so crowded spectra come apart. NMR is an insensitive technique because the nuclear magneton is small, and field is the remedy.

Problem 2: The magnetic field of a sunspot¶

In 1908 George Ellery Hale found that spectral lines from sunspots are split, and used the Zeeman effect to measure a magnetic field beyond the Earth for the first time. An iron line at 630.25 nm splits into three components shifted by 0 and ±g μBB\pm g\,\mu_BB±gμB​B, with g=2.5g = 2.5g=2.5 for this line. In a large sunspot each outer component lies 0.014 nm from the center. (a) Find the field. (b) Compare it with the Earth’s field, 5×10−55\times10^{-5}5×10−5 T. (c) A spectrograph has a resolving power λ/Δλ=500 000\lambda/\Delta\lambda = 500\,000λ/Δλ=500000. What is the weakest field whose splitting it can resolve with this line?

Problem 3: A spin pointing at an angle¶

Consider the spin state χ=cos⁡θ2 α+sin⁡θ2 β\chi = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\,\alpha + \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,\betaχ=cos2θ​α+sin2θ​β. (a) Show that it is normalized. (b) What are the probabilities of the two readings of SzS_zSz​? (c) Find ⟨Sz⟩\langle S_z\rangle⟨Sz​⟩, ⟨Sx⟩\langle S_x\rangle⟨Sx​⟩ and ⟨Sy⟩\langle S_y\rangle⟨Sy​⟩, and say in which direction the spin points on average. (d) Show that χ\chiχ is an eigenvector of the spin component along that direction, S^θ=S^zcos⁡θ+S^xsin⁡θ\hat{S}_\theta = \hat{S}_z\cos\theta + \hat{S}_x\sin\thetaS^θ​=S^z​cosθ+S^x​sinθ. (e) A beam prepared in α\alphaα enters a Stern-Gerlach magnet tilted by θ\thetaθ from zzz. What fraction comes out +++? Check 0°, 90°, 180° and 60° against the widget.

Solution

(a) ∣cα∣2+∣cβ∣2=cos⁡2θ2+sin⁡2θ2=1\lvert c_\alpha\rvert^2 + \lvert c_\beta\rvert^2 = \cos^2\frac{\theta}{2} + \sin^2\frac{\theta}{2} = 1∣cα​∣2+∣cβ​∣2=cos22θ​+sin22θ​=1.

(b) P(+12ℏ)=cos⁡2θ2P(+\frac{1}{2}\hbar) = \cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}P(+21​ℏ)=cos22θ​ and P(−12ℏ)=sin⁡2θ2P(-\frac{1}{2}\hbar) = \sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}P(−21​ℏ)=sin22θ​.

(c) With c=cos⁡θ2c = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}c=cos2θ​ and s=sin⁡θ2s = \sin\frac{\theta}{2}s=sin2θ​:

⟨Sz⟩=12ℏ (c2−s2)=12ℏcos⁡θ\langle S_z\rangle = \tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\,(c^2 - s^2) = \tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\cos\theta⟨Sz​⟩=21​ℏ(c2−s2)=21​ℏcosθ
(54)
⟨Sx⟩=ℏ2(cs)(0110)(cs)=12ℏ (2cs)=12ℏsin⁡θ\langle S_x\rangle = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}c & s\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}c\\ s\end{pmatrix} = \tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\,(2cs) = \tfrac{1}{2}\hbar\sin\theta⟨Sx​⟩=2ℏ​(c​s​)(01​10​)(cs​)=21​ℏ(2cs)=21​ℏsinθ
(55)

and ⟨Sy⟩=12ℏ (−i cs+i sc)=0\langle S_y\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\hbar\,(-i\,cs + i\,sc) = 0⟨Sy​⟩=21​ℏ(−ics+isc)=0. The averages are the components of an arrow of length 12ℏ\frac{1}{2}\hbar21​ℏ in the xzxzxz plane, tilted by θ\thetaθ from the zzz axis.

(d) Row times column, then the formulas for the cosine and sine of a difference:

S^θ χ=ℏ2(cos⁡θsin⁡θsin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)(cs)=ℏ2(cos⁡θcos⁡θ2+sin⁡θsin⁡θ2sin⁡θcos⁡θ2−cos⁡θsin⁡θ2)\hat{S}_\theta\,\chi = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta & \sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & -\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}c\\ s\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta\cos\frac{\theta}{2} + \sin\theta\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\[2pt] \sin\theta\cos\frac{\theta}{2} - \cos\theta\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\end{pmatrix}S^θ​χ=2ℏ​(cosθsinθ​sinθ−cosθ​)(cs​)=2ℏ​(cosθcos2θ​+sinθsin2θ​sinθcos2θ​−cosθsin2θ​​)
(56)
=ℏ2(cos⁡(θ−θ2)sin⁡(θ−θ2))=ℏ2(cs)=+ℏ2 χ= \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\cos\left(\theta - \frac{\theta}{2}\right)\\[2pt] \sin\left(\theta - \frac{\theta}{2}\right)\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar}{2}\begin{pmatrix}c\\ s\end{pmatrix} = +\frac{\hbar}{2}\,\chi=2ℏ​(cos(θ−2θ​)sin(θ−2θ​)​)=2ℏ​(cs​)=+2ℏ​χ
(57)

χ\chiχ is “spin up along the tilted axis”. For θ=90°\theta = 90°θ=90° it is χ+x=(α+β)/2\chi_{+x} = (\alpha + \beta)/\sqrt{2}χ+x​=(α+β)/2​.

(e) The magnet measures SθS_\thetaSθ​, and the probability of its +++ reading is the squared component of α\alphaα along χ\chiχ: ∣⟨χ∣α⟩∣2=cos⁡2θ2\lvert\langle\chi|\alpha\rangle\rvert^2 = \cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}∣⟨χ∣α⟩∣2=cos22θ​. That gives 1 at 0°, 12\frac{1}{2}21​ at 90°, 0 at 180° and cos⁡230°=0.75\cos^230° = 0.75cos230°=0.75 at 60°. The half angle is the mark of spin 12\frac{1}{2}21​: the state orthogonal to “up” is reached by turning the axis through 180°, not 90°.

Problem 5: How strong is the magnet inside an atom?¶

The spin-orbit splitting of a p level can be read as the energy needed to turn the spin moment over in an internal magnetic field, ΔE≈2μBBint\Delta E \approx 2\mu_BB_{\text{int}}ΔE≈2μB​Bint​. (a) Estimate BintB_{\text{int}}Bint​ for hydrogen’s 2p level, which is split by 0.365 cm−1^{-1}−1. (b) Do the same for sodium’s 3p level (17.2 cm−1^{-1}−1) and caesium’s 6p level (554 cm−1^{-1}−1). (c) For which of hydrogen and sodium is a 1 T laboratory magnet a “weak” field, and what does each atom’s spectrum show in it?

Solution

(a) With μB/hc=0.467\mu_B/hc = 0.467μB​/hc=0.467 cm−1^{-1}−1/T:

Bint=Δν~2 μB/hc=0.365 cm−12×0.467 cm−1/T=0.39 TB_{\text{int}} = \frac{\Delta\tilde{\nu}}{2\,\mu_B/hc} = \frac{0.365\ \text{cm}^{-1}}{2\times0.467\ \text{cm}^{-1}/\text{T}} = 0.39\ \text{T}Bint​=2μB​/hcΔν~​=2×0.467 cm−1/T0.365 cm−1​=0.39 T
(58)

(b) Sodium: 17.2/0.934=1817.2/0.934 = 1817.2/0.934=18 T. Caesium: 554/0.934=590554/0.934 = 590554/0.934=590 T. The strongest steady laboratory magnets reach about 45 T, so the outer electron of a heavy atom lives in a field that no laboratory can supply.

(c) A field is weak when μBB\mu_BBμB​B is small compared with the spin-orbit splitting, that is when B≪BintB \ll B_{\text{int}}B≪Bint​. For sodium 1 T is weak (1≪181 \ll 181≪18): jjj and mjm_jmj​ label the states, and the D lines show the anomalous Zeeman pattern. For hydrogen 1 T is already larger than the internal 0.4 T: mlm_lml​ and msm_sms​ are nearly sharp, and the lines are close to the normal triplet. The same magnet puts the two atoms at opposite ends of the figure in “Weak field or strong field”.

Problem 7: The 21 cm line¶

The proton has spin I=12I = \frac{1}{2}I=21​. In the ground state of hydrogen the magnetic moments of the proton and the electron are coupled by a term A′ I⃗^⋅S⃗^/ℏ2A'\,\hat{\vec{I}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}}/\hbar^2A′I^⋅S^/ℏ2, the hyperfine interaction, of the same form as spin-orbit coupling. The total angular momentum is F⃗^=I⃗^+S⃗^\hat{\vec{F}} = \hat{\vec{I}} + \hat{\vec{S}}F^=I^+S^. (a) What values can FFF take, and how many states does each have? (b) Find the energy of each level in terms of A′A'A′. (c) The measured gap is 1420.406 MHz. Find the wavelength and the photon energy, and compare the energy with the fine structure of 2p. (d) In an interstellar cloud at 100 K, what fraction of the hydrogen atoms is in the upper level?

Solution

(a) Two spins 12\frac{1}{2}21​ add like lll and sss: F=12+12=1F = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = 1F=21​+21​=1 or 12−12=0\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} = 021​−21​=0. F=1F = 1F=1 has three states (mF=1,0,−1m_F = 1, 0, -1mF​=1,0,−1) and F=0F = 0F=0 has one: 3+1=4=2×23 + 1 = 4 = 2\times23+1=4=2×2.

(b) The squaring trick again, I⃗^⋅S⃗^=12(F^2−I^2−S^2)\hat{\vec{I}}\cdot\hat{\vec{S}} = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{F}^2 - \hat{I}^2 - \hat{S}^2)I^⋅S^=21​(F^2−I^2−S^2):

EF=A′2[F(F+1)−34−34]={+14A′F=1−34A′F=0E_F = \frac{A'}{2}\left[F(F+1) - \tfrac{3}{4} - \tfrac{3}{4}\right] = \begin{cases} +\frac{1}{4}A' & F = 1\\[2pt] -\frac{3}{4}A' & F = 0\end{cases}EF​=2A′​[F(F+1)−43​−43​]={+41​A′−43​A′​F=1F=0​
(59)

The gap is A′A'A′, and the center does not move: 3×14−1×34=03\times\frac{1}{4} - 1\times\frac{3}{4} = 03×41​−1×43​=0.

(c) λ=c/ν=2.998×108/1.4204×109=0.211\lambda = c/\nu = 2.998\times10^{8}/1.4204\times10^{9} = 0.211λ=c/ν=2.998×108/1.4204×109=0.211 m =21.1= 21.1=21.1 cm, and hν=5.9×10−6h\nu = 5.9\times10^{-6}hν=5.9×10−6 eV. The fine structure of 2p is 4.5×10−54.5\times10^{-5}4.5×10−5 eV, eight times larger: the proton’s moment is far weaker than the electron’s.

(d) kBT=8.6×10−3k_BT = 8.6\times10^{-3}kB​T=8.6×10−3 eV at 100 K, 1500 times the gap, so the Boltzmann factor is 1 and the populations follow the number of states, 3 to 1: three quarters of the atoms are in F=1F = 1F=1. An atom in F=1F = 1F=1 radiates only about once in 107 years, but there is so much hydrogen between the stars that the line, first detected in 1951, maps the spiral arms of the galaxy.
